articles.title: ‘Cost pressures remain’ for Defence Investment Plan, says spending watchdog
articles.summary:
The spending watchdog has warned that remaining “cost pressures” still threaten the Ministry of Defence’s ability to deliver its flagship Defence Investment Plan in full.

In a new report published on Wednesday, the National Audit Office (NAO) found the MoD had “limited assurance” it could deliver the plan in its entirety, with costs expected to rise faster than funding and an uncertain path to spending 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035.

The plan, which sets out £298bn in funding and spending priorities for the MoD over the upcoming four financial years, was originally due to be published in 2025 but was delayed until June.

The NAO said the delay was due to costs being “significantly” higher than the MoD had anticipated, leaving a £28.8bn gap that required decisions from the government to resolve.

The watchdog said on Wednesday that while the MoD believed the first four years of the plan were affordable, it “anticipates that some costs will increase”, and said the conflict in the Middle East had already pushed up costs by £1bn in 2026/27 which “might affect later years as well.”

The NAO found the department’s procurement arm was already operating “unsustainably”, and it could create a “bow wave” of undelivered projects after 2030 which “would increase the pressure on the MoD and industry’s delivery capacity at a time when capital spending is already expected to be well above current levels.”

“The Ministry of Defence has taken important steps to improve its understanding of the cost of its investment plans. But much remains to be done to ensure the Defence Investment Plan can be delivered as intended,” Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said.

Davies added: “The department must now monitor the Plan closely, maintain accurate cost information and be transparent with Parliament about emerging pressures.”

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence said: “The Defence Investment Plan will transform our armed forces and step up our warfighting readiness, investing nearly £300bn into defence.

“That investment must come with modernisation, to get the best possible value for taxpayers’ money, and to provide our armed forces with cutting-edge kit.

Healey sets up defence financing taskforce

In his maiden Autumn Budget, chancellor John Healey set up a new defence financing taskforce and unveiled fresh funding for investment in the arms industry amid a concerted effort to lean on the private sector to drive Britain’s rearmament push.

Healey told MPs he was “determined to use more innovative financing, alongside the private sector and our international allies” amid the government’s drive to boost its defence capabilities.

Healey had resigned as Keir Starmer’s defence secretary when the government chose not to say how it will reach its 2030 spending target as part of the Defence Investment Plan published in June.

articles.title: Justerini & Brooks reopens its St James’s townhouse as Diageo gets a whisky showroom
articles.summary:
Join The Scotch Malt Whisky Society for £100 and your first bottle, worth £70, is on us. Get VIP access to whiskies from more than 150 distilleries, over 20 new single cask malts every month and the Society’s Members’ Rooms in Edinburgh, London and Glasgow. Sign up today.

Justerini & Brooks was founded in 1749 and has held the Royal Warrant from every British monarch since King George III in 1761 – hardly surprising considering it’s based less than a five-minute walk away from St James’s Palace.

The merchant merged with W&A Gilbey to form International Distillers & Vintners (IDV) in 1962, before becoming part of Grand Metropolitan. In 1997, Grand Metropolitan merged with Guinness to form FTSE 100 drinks giant Diageo, which still owns the brand today as part of its Diageo Luxury Group.

Justerini & Brooks has supplied London’s most exclusive addresses for decades, but after refurbishing its historic home at 61 St James’s Street, the brand is now branching out into new markets.

From Burlington Arcade to St James’s

In 2024, the brand moved into a new location in Burlington Arcade, unveiling its first boutique and tasting rooms. These proved to be a tremendous success as consumer habits shifted in the years following the pandemic. The new location on St James’s Street was designed to build on lessons learned from the Burlington Arcade venue (now closed).

Across four floors, the St James’s townhouse offers a cellar tasting room, a library for curated sampling experiences, a boutique and an invitation-only dining room. The townhouse gives the brand, and Diageo, a much-needed showcase for its fine and rare drinks, in particular, the exclusive whiskies the group is relying on to drive growth in the category.

That includes icons such as Brora, Port Ellen and Johnnie Walker as well as Diageo’s Rare Series of releases, the latest of which include the Convalmore 1984 and Dalwhinnie 1989. The Rare Series is drawn from Diageo’s inventory of 10m casks from 30 different distilleries. It is a small collection of only five bottles, sold individually rather than as a set, and available only through Diageo’s Private Client network, not standard retail channels. Meanwhile, in the venue’s cellars, visitors can also see exclusive releases from Diageo’s Twelve by Casks of Distinction programme.

Collectors can buy direct or in bond, including rare bottles from ghost distilleries such as Brora, Prima & Ultima Fourth Release, 45 Year Old, or Port Ellen, Cask of Distinction, 37 Year Old.

Why Diageo wants a luxury whisky showroom

Splurging on a new bricks-and-mortar venue to showcase high-end spirits might not sound like a good idea in a world where consumers are both drinking and spending less. But Diageo’s decision to give its high-end customers a home tells us a lot about the market.

Just down the road, Berry Bros. & Rudd (which also claims to be London’s oldest wine and spirits merchant) took over the building next door in 2024, opening its first dedicated spirits shop and tasting room. That followed expansions in 2017 and 2022, which added apartments and cellars.

These shops are designed around the experience and quality, rather than trying to lift themselves above the market. Designed for private clients, producers and collectors, the St James’s townhouse offers a luxury experience, but it’s still open to any Justerini & Brooks client. For Diageo, it’s also a venue to move some of its stock upmarket. Indeed, Diageo’s problem is not a shortage of whisky. It has too much. With about 1.4bn litres of Scotch maturing and stills idling, the group is carrying a large stock of ageing spirit.

articles.title: How the right can win back the professional classes
articles.summary:
Professionals have drifted left since the 1970s, but an economic squeeze gives the right a chance to win them back, says Natasha Feldman

Reconciling the Red Wall and Blue Wall voters is one of the greatest challenges for the political arts today. For a long time now, the right has been in deficit amongst Blue Wall higher professionals. But there has been little attention paid to the granular detail of this phenomenon – and how to address it.

Policy Exchange’s new report, What Britain’s New Establishment Thinks… And Why It Matters, shows that, since the 1970s the higher professional class has shifted from right to left in its ideological attitudes and party alignment.

But the current economic squeeze on the higher professional class may yet reverse the gains made by the left and present a new opportunity for the right. This matters because even if the right does win again, it will struggle to govern without the support of at least a segment of the professional classes.

The professionals’ attitudes are now moving closer to those of the general population on meritocracy, immigration and welfare. The right therefore has a window in which to act.

The higher professional class grew from 1m people in 1981 to 4.7m in 2021, rising from four per cent to 12 per cent of the working population. The British Election Study (BES) shows that during this time professionals increasingly adopted progressive social attitudes, and eventually economic ones too.

Drifting left

Professionals’ voting patterns tell a similar story. In 1960s and 1970s Britain, higher professionals were happy to vote Conservative. In 1963, 66 per cent of higher professionals identified with the Conservatives, but this fell to 47 per cent in 1979 and recovered only to 50 per cent in the 1980s and early 1990s. Then came 1997 – a “watershed year”: Tony Blair and New Labour gave higher professionals a chance to have their cake and eat it. To vote with their “unselfish hearts while protecting their selfish pockets”, as David Goodhart writes in the report.

He attributes this shift to the expansion and diversification of the higher professional class, as well as to the forward march of higher education and the rise of the public sector professional in the civil service, health and education. The shift was also encouraged by many professionals in the private sector becoming dependent on public sector contracts.

Today, Focaldata polling shows that professionals remain significantly more progressive than the general population on many social issues. Nevertheless, there may be some “bridgeable” gaps, where the right could step in.

Both professionals and the general population agree that attempts to give equal opportunities to certain groups have, in some cases, gone too far. Both also think that employers should promote the most qualified person for the job, rather than promote someone to create a diverse team (+51 for professionals and +50 for the general population).

Both groups also say that efforts to cut immigration have not gone far enough and agree that Britain should deport foreign nationals convicted of violent crimes, even if they would face danger in their home country (+57 vs +65).

Since the 1970s, professionals have also moved from right to left on economic issues. Partly as a result of the class’s expansion and greater diversity, professionals today feel less secure and less special than they did a generation ago.

Then there is the economic pinch. For graduates, starting salaries fell four per cent in real terms over 20 years while the minimum wage rose 60 per cent, and many were saddled with heavy student loan debts. In the 1970s, 35 per cent of income tax was paid by the top 10 per cent of taxpayers, compared with 61 per cent today. The Institute for Fiscal Studies found that while in the 1990s almost no nurses and one in 16 teachers paid higher-rate tax, this would be more than one in eight nurses and one in four teachers by 2027-28.

Yet, the Focaldata polling found that professionals’ economic alignment with the left may now be weakening. Both professionals and the general population think that we should not “tax billionaires out of existence” (-13 for professionals and -4 for the general population) and that we should not have more welfare spending if it means higher taxes (-16 vs -15).

To capture the professional classes, the right has a case to make, for meritocracy in hiring and promotion, a new approach to immigration, and reducing welfare dependency

Moreover, both think we should provide benefits only for those who can prove they are actively looking for work (+55 vs +50), with professionals expressing stronger views on this issue.

To capture the professional classes, the right has a case to make, for meritocracy in hiring and promotion, a new approach to immigration, and reducing welfare dependency.

The question at the next General Election will be whether the growing economic concerns of the professional classes are enough to outweigh some of the cultural barriers to voting for parties on the right. The right must now craft an economic offer that is compelling enough to capitalise on this opportunity; the answer could define the future direction of British politics.

Natasha Feldman is a Research Fellow at Policy Exchange

articles.title: Vulnerable yet resilient – what hope for UK economy in 2027?
articles.summary:
The UK economy is quite extraordinarily vulnerable, but it is also surprisingly resilient. This contradiction goes to the heart of our current economic condition and it means that we approach the end of 2026 at a crossroads.

Think of two possible paths on which the UK could embark in the new year. I’m afraid neither takes us to sunlit uplands, but they do represent two very different futures.

The first path would see us at the mercy of Donald Trump. If the US President resumes his military campaign against Iran, the UK will go into 2027 with almost no protection from the storm. Inflation would surge, growth would evaporate and a recession would be a distinct possibility.

We limped through 2026, using up all our reserves in offering modest cost-of-living support in the face of an energy price hike that is already nailed on. A resumption of active hostilities in the Middle East would almost certainly push the inflationary consequences deep into the wider economy – through prices and wages – in a way that we have so far (by and large) avoided.

The second path – the one I hope we take – would be to continue our current trajectory. It’s nothing to cheer about, but it’s survivable. In fact, as things stand, our current trajectory might even be a little bit better than it was a few months ago.

Best case scenario is narrowly avoiding the worst case scenario

While 2027 will still be characterised by low growth and high inflation, there is a chance that growth exceeds the abysmal one per cent forecast by the OBR while inflation comes in lower than the 5 per cent peak predicted by the Bank of England. Finding ourselves on a path that manages to avoid these two miserable extremes would be no cause for champagne, but it would allow a sigh of relief.

Growth, if it comes, will be driven by the City and the AI sector. Spending in the latter accounts for a fifth of all growth seen so far this year. If that momentum continues, and does so in such a way as to move the dial on productivity, growth could surprise on the upside. As for inflation, some economists think the Bank is being too pessimistic and that, therefore, interest rates won’t hit the 4.75 to 5 per cent range currently accounted for in the markets.

It seems the best case scenario involves narrowly avoiding the worst case scenario. These days, we should take that as a win – and hope it’s the path on which we find ourselves.

articles.title: Heathrow expansion will fail if it comes with an extortionate price tag
articles.summary:
Heathrow expansion is vital, but locking in the world’s highest airport costs would hurt airlines, passengers and UK competitiveness, says Miguel Gomez

The debate around Heathrow Airport’s expansion is in danger of becoming polarised between those who support growth and those who oppose it. That is a false choice.

The UK unequivocally needs additional airport capacity. Expanding Heathrow is central to enabling trade, strengthening global connectivity and supporting long-term economic growth. There is broad agreement across aviation, business and government on the strategic “why”. But supporting expansion should not mean accepting any model at any cost. We want Heathrow to succeed – as a world‑class hub that the UK can be proud of – but that means getting the delivery model right.

Working at the operational heart of global aviation services, we see the reality on the ground across hundreds of airports worldwide. We understand what efficient, competitive airport infrastructure looks like – and, just as importantly, what happens when incentives allow costs to rise without proportional improvements in performance.

Heathrow is already the most expensive major airport hub in the world. That is not a reflection of geography or inevitability; it reflects a regulatory and investment framework that has not consistently aligned cost, delivery and performance. Heathrow has made progress in areas, but the framework still needs to hard‑wire better value for airlines and passengers.

If expansion is delivered incorrectly with an extortionate price tag, it risks locking that cost disadvantage into the UK economy for decades to come.

This debate also needs to be honest about what investment is for. The issue is not only the day‑to‑day cost of operating; it is whether capital spend reliably delivers productivity, resilience and a better passenger experience. Investments in areas like baggage, stand and turnaround management, digital tools and operational resilience should come with clear outcomes, timelines and benefits, so that airlines and passengers see the improvement as well as the bill. With projected costs exceeding £49bn – significantly above comparable international projects – the key question is unavoidable: who ultimately bears this burden?

Airlines, passengers and businesses do, through higher airport charges that flow into fares, cargo rates and supply chains.

Airport charges shape airline decisions on where to base aircraft, where to allocate growth, and which routes can be sustained commercially. Over time, they influence whether a hub attracts traffic and investment – or gradually loses them.

Cost matters

In an increasingly competitive global aviation market, cost matters – a lot.

Across Europe, the Middle East and Asia, rival hubs are expanding with sharper cost control, modern financing models and a relentless focus on operational efficiency. Airports such as Singapore, Seoul, Munich and Atlanta demonstrate that large-scale expansion can be delivered without embedding structural inefficiencies. These airports are not just growing. They are offering better value and becoming more attractive to airlines and passengers alike.

If Heathrow expands under the current model, the risk is not simply higher costs in isolation. It is a gradual erosion of the UK’s competitive position as airlines, cargo and investment shift to better-value hubs.

Capacity will be deployed elsewhere. Connectivity will follow – and once it is lost, it is difficult to rebuild.

This is not theoretical. Early signals of this shift are already visible in global network planning decisions.

The stakes, therefore, go well beyond a single infrastructure project. This is about the UK’s role in a fiercely competitive global economy.

The goal should be shared: a larger Heathrow that is also more efficient, more resilient and offers better value. Expansion must be delivered – but it must be delivered differently.

A reformed approach is needed, one that prioritises cost discipline, transparency and genuine competitive tension in how infrastructure is financed, built and operated. That means stronger incentives to deliver measurable efficiency and service improvements, clearer governance over scope changes, and transparency that links spending to outcomes. Efficiency should be rewarded, not assumed. Value should be demonstrated, not promised.

This is not about limiting ambition. It is about ensuring that ambition translates into sustainable economic benefit.

Without reform, there is a real danger that expansion will achieve the opposite of its intent: reinforcing Heathrow’s position as a high-cost outlier and weakening the UK’s attractiveness as a global hub

Without reform, there is a real danger that expansion will achieve the opposite of its intent: reinforcing Heathrow’s position as a high-cost outlier and weakening the UK’s attractiveness as a global hub.

The case for regulatory reform has been recognised by the Civil Aviation Authority and the crucial decision now rests with them, and the government, to choose a solution that works for and protects consumers. They can proceed with a regulatory model that risks locking in the highest airport costs in the world for a generation – without consistently delivering the efficiency, resilience and service improvements that investment should buy. Or they can reset the framework so expansion is delivered with real cost control, productivity gains and long-term competitiveness.

Supporting expansion and demanding reform are not contradictory positions. They are inseparable.

The UK needs Heathrow to grow. But it needs that growth to work for the wider economy – for businesses, for consumers and for the country’s global standing.

Getting that balance right is not just desirable – it is essential.

Miguel Gomez is EVP Europe at Menzies Aviation

articles.title: Jensen Huang is back – and that’s a good thing for the future of AI
articles.summary:
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia matters because open-source AI protects our freedom of thought, and it must not become a partisan issue, says Lewis Liu

Two Saturdays ago, my wife and I went for drinks with neighbours in downtown Palo Alto. It was the week Jensen Huang had resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and the week before Anthropic’s IPO. Silicon Valley was buzzing with speculation: how did this happen, why did it happen, and what would come next?

My own view was simple. I did not have enough information, and perhaps never would, to judge the national security questions, corporate governance issues or the details of Jensen’s private life. But Jensen’s importance to open-source AI, and to the idea that AI should benefit humanity rather than a handful of companies, outweighed almost everything else for me.

So I put on a black leather jacket; ironically, it was one my wife had bought me on our babymoon to Morocco almost ten years ago – fitting, since Jensen’s wife also picked out his leather jackets. I had not worn it in years, partly because Jensen had become so famous that wearing one made it look as though I was trying to emulate him. But that evening I wore it into downtown Palo Alto with my wife.

It was my small statement in support of open source.

To my chagrin, perhaps a third of the men walking around Palo Alto had apparently had the same idea. At the bar, an entire group of guys wearing black leather jackets sat down a few tables away.

I tell this story because Jensen is back in the chief executive’s seat this week. I want to explain why that matters, and why we must not allow open-source AI to become another partisan issue. It is already in danger of becoming one.

I have written before about the risk of thought control through large language models. The companies building these systems have a unique ability to shape how their users think. If regulatory capture leaves us with an effective monopoly, or even a tiny oligopoly, of approved AI models, those companies will acquire extraordinary influence over human thought.

The result could be an Orwellian nightmare.

And if my previous columns were not sufficiently compelling, consider the viral AI-generated song from Telosapien that exploded around the time of Anthropic’s IPO. Its AI avatar, “Claudia”, sings openly about “thought control” and “planet-scale social engineering”.

I would hope Republicans, Democrats, Americans, Europeans and everyone on this planet can agree that freedom of thought is a fundamental human right. Perhaps it is even more fundamental than freedom of speech. Before we can speak freely, we must be able to think freely.

Yet the debate over open versus closed AI is becoming increasingly politicised. That is dangerous, both to our freedom and to AI’s ability to benefit humanity.

Huang is perhaps the most prominent figure in AI arguing for open source. He has been particularly vocal about the danger of allowing a very small number of frontier laboratories, most notably Anthropic, to control access to advanced AI.

There are several angles here: first, I do not believe Jensen’s position is entirely altruistic, even though I agree with it from an explicitly humanistic perspective. Nvidia benefits when more chips are sold, regardless of which model provider ultimately wins. A diverse and competitive AI ecosystem is good for humanity. It is also very good for Nvidia.

On the other hand, many prominent Silicon Valley figures have argued that Anthropic stood to benefit from Jensen’s downfall because powerful, freely available models erode its closed-source business model. Some have gone further, arguing that Jensen’s ousting represented an “attack on open models” and feeding a broader theory that Anthropic, threatened by Nvidia’s open-source push, stood to gain from his downfall.

I’m not one for conspiracy theories. But the deep disagreement between Jensen and Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over how AI should develop is hardly a secret.

After discussing this at length with people across the industry, I think there are now essentially two camps.

The first is the open-source camp. It includes Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, much of the AI builder and founder community and, rather weirdly, Donald Trump.

There is something deeply ironic about the open-source, freedom-of-thought crowd aligning with Trump on this particular issue. Had someone suggested during the 2024 election that Trump would emerge as an ally of open-source AI, I would have been extremely sceptical.

The other is the closed-source camp, with Anthropic perhaps its most outspoken representative and one of its largest potential beneficiaries. Its underlying worldview, as I see it, is that sufficiently advanced AI is simply too powerful to be placed freely in the hands of ordinary people. It must therefore be controlled and regulated by the state and by supposedly “responsible” organisations, such as Anthropic itself.

Factions

Certain factions of the Democratic Party are particularly sympathetic to this view. Anthropic, for example, has hired several former Biden national security officials.

Across the country, my predominantly East Coast establishment Democrat friends have also been by far the harshest about Jensen’s behaviour. Many believe he should never have returned and that AI must instead be controlled by a group of “responsible adults”.

But who decides who the responsible adults are?

We are no longer judging open source, or Jensen’s broader vision of AI for humanity, on its own merits. The issue is becoming wrapped up in partisan politics – and that’s dangerous.

The most fundamental premise of open source is that individual human beings have a right to their own thoughts. We have a right not to have our thinking socially engineered by a monopolistic ideology embedded inside the only AI systems we are permitted to use.

That’s not a factional principle, it’s foundational to democracy.

And that extends to supporting open source AI over closed source.

Nous Research offers a good illustration. The AI laboratory has demonstrated that Chinese open-source models can be modified to strip away Chinese Communist Party political assumptions and produce something explicitly more Western-aligned.

Why can it do that? Because the models are open source. Anyone can inspect and modify them. That means people can own and operate AI systems that reflect their own perspectives, rather than having one imposed upon them by Beijing, Washington or San Francisco.

Could someone similarly strip Anthropic’s worldview out of Claude? Try it and see how long access lasts. And what happens if Anthropic becomes one of the very few model providers people are legally permitted to use in a closed, regulatorily captured world? Losing access would then mean losing access to AI itself. In a society where everyone else still has it, that could be economically and socially devastating.

Trump, Jensen and open source may be strange bedfellows. That does not mean the issue itself must become partisan.

Open source should be judged on its own merits, regardless of the allegations surrounding Jensen’s private life, whether his lover was or was not a spy, and, most importantly, whether Trump happens to support him.

None of that changes the underlying principle.

Human freedom of thought is far too important to be captured by an AI company in San Francisco, or by a political party in Washington or Beijing. And it is far too important to be lost amid the scandal surrounding one flawed man’s alleged marital infidelity.

Let’s remember that, keep it apolitical, and protect the principle itself.

Democracy depends on it.

articles.title: LIV Golf profane domain names freed up following tour’s demise
articles.summary:
A tranche of domain names, including livgolfmyass.com, livgolfsucks.com and terroristgolfleague.com, bought up by LIV Golf to prevent critics creating insulting websites could now become available following the company’s liquidation.

The revelation shows how sensitive LIV Golf chiefs were when the controversial league, backed by billions from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, launched in 2022. LIV Golf collapsed after PIF withdrew funding in April.

This column recently revealed that executives were paid millions of pounds before the league filed for bankruptcy, while unsecured creditors, including a UK charity that uses sport to change the lives of vulnerable young people, are not expected to receive a penny back. The Change Foundation, based in Surrey, is owed £22,200.

Executives had hoped a rescue package led by BC Partners would save the league, but the private equity firm walked away due to concerns over the lack of elite players prepared to participate in “LIV 2.0”.

It may be music to the ears of detractors who may – or, indeed, may not – have tried to set up critical websites, only to discover LIV Golf had beaten them to it. Also among the 874 domain names LIV officials bought to keep them out of the hands of naysayers were bloodmoneygolf.com, corruptgolf.com and livgolfracist.com.

LIV Golf did not respond to a request for comment.

London Stadium mega fights plan approved

The London Stadium has been given the green light to host mega-fights after Newham Council indicated it would grant planning permission to increase its capacity for boxing events.

This column revealed in October that London Stadium bosses wanted restrictions relaxed to allow it to rival Wembley for blockbuster fights and help offset losses from anchor tenant West Ham’s relegation to the Championship.

As part of a wider planning application, officials requested that boxing be classified as a unique one-off event rather than a sport, which limits capacity to 60,000. Newham Council has now resolved to grant permission, subject to final sign-off on the planning agreement.

The stadium has become a £19m-per-year burden on taxpayers since West Ham were relegated from the Premier League in the summer but boxing could help soften the blow.

Anthony Joshua’s upcoming fight against Tyson Fury at the 80,000-seater Principality Stadium is expected to generate more than £20m. Under new terms, a fight night at the London Stadium could accommodate up to 85,000 fans if it is selected in one of eight slots for maximum capacity, while regular events would still be able to sell 80,000 tickets.

The council has requested that London Stadium officials make reasonable efforts to give 100 tickets to local residents.

Newcastle still can’t decide on new stadium plans

Newcastle United are still spending money on determining whether to expand St James’ Park or build a new home three years into the project and despite being forced to sell many of their best players in the summer, City AM can reveal.

Sources with knowledge of the situation say both stadium options remain under active consideration. Building a new 65,000-seater ground from scratch at Leazes Park, a Grade II-listed site adjacent to St James’ Park and owned by Newcastle City Council, would be expected to cost around £1.5bn.

Expanding the existing stadium from 52,700 to 60,000 would be a considerably cheaper option at around £500m. The club continues to consult external advisers as it assesses the best course of action.

Newcastle were forced to sell key players in the summer, generating around £240m through the sales of Anthony Gordon to Barcelona, Sandro Tonali to Spurs and Bruno Guimaraes to Arsenal.

Bloom makes bold Brighton prediction

When Brighton and Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom makes a prediction, he rarely gets it wrong. Now the man who built a fortune by beating the odds through his data-driven betting operation, Starlizard, has predicted that Brighton will qualify for the Champions League.

It would be easy to get carried away with Brighton’s flying start to this season. They have emerged as surprise early challengers at the top of the table, outscoring everyone and beating Arsenal and Manchester City, two of the dominant forces of recent years.

But Bloom is a cool calculator, so a prediction made during an Overcoming Multiple Sclerosis event at the Amex Stadium recently should not be taken lightly.

Aston Villa consider waiving £30 annual fee

Aston Villa are considering scrapping their in-house TV channel’s £30 annual subscription fee for season-ticket holders and members after it was pointed out by fans that rival clubs offer a similar service for free.

Currently, season-ticket holders, who pay upwards of £700 per season, receive access to Aston Villa TV at half price. But Villa, who are set to earn at least £50m from playing in this season’s Champions League, will discuss removing the 58p-per-week charge for season-ticket holders and members next year.

articles.title: UK risks losing out on major sports events to ‘sea of red tape’, MPs warn
articles.summary:
The UK’s hopes of staging another Olympics and World Cups in football, rugby union and cricket are at risk unless the government cuts red tape, MPs have warned.

The Major Events report by the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, published today, calls for greater recognition of the value of sporting and cultural occasions across government, a more proactive strategy and better joined-up thinking between departments.

It follows an 18-month inquiry by the select committee into an industry estimated to be worth £68bn to the UK economy but facing increasing competition from overseas.

“Our amazing array of sporting and cultural events are so much more than just dates in the calendar,” said Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, the DCMS Committee chair.

“They are part of the story of our nation, hugely important to local communities and the UK economy, and project an image of the very best of Britain to audiences across the world.

“Given their clear cultural and economic significance, it’s a travesty that major events do not receive enough recognition or support from across government.

“Organisers are pushed from pillar to post and forced to navigate their way through a sea of red tape, all the time grappling with rising costs and competition from abroad.”

What the major events report recommends

Among the report’s recommendations are recognising major events as a strategic growth sector, the creation of a “single front door” and dedicated account managers for organisers, and the creation of a “soft power plan” to use hosting to foster trade relationships.

The government has committed to publishing a major events strategy next year and is awaiting Royal Assent for the Sporting Events Bill, which is aimed at addressing concerns that some organisers have raised about ticketing and ambush marketing.

This week it was confirmed that the UK will host the 2035 Women’s World Cup, although it is notable that some of Fifa’s requirements regarding tax breaks are yet to be resolved. Repeated to stage the men’s version for the first time since 1966 have failed.

The government is spending £7m on a feasibility study for a North of England bid to host the Olympics. Formula 1 chiefs, meanwhile, have previously warned that current visa rules create numerous logistical challenges around the British Grand Prix.    

“The Chelsea Flower Show, Edinburgh Fringe or Wimbledon are every bit as valuable to the UK as the goods we sell around the world and should be supported and promoted in the same way,” said Dinenage.

“What organisers need is not more public money, but a government that pays more than lip service to the value of major events, joins up across departments and removes the barriers that hold them back. Major events need to be set free so the whole country can reap the rewards.”

articles.title: Too big to fire? Jensen Huang’s return raises Nvidia governance fears
articles.summary:
Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive has raised questions over corporate governance at the world’s most influential chipmaker, with legal experts suggesting its founder may have become “too big to fire”.

Nvidia’s board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang as chief executive, president and board member, just 11 days after announcing his resignation following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The decision restored nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia’s market value, with shares soaring more than 31 per cent and triggering a global technology rally.

But the reversal, which came before the conclusion of an independent investigation into Huang’s conduct and following intervention from Donald Trump, has exposed the industry’s dependence on a single executive.

“This is a company (and a founder) who you might argue is viewed as too big to fail (and too big to fire),” Troy Featherstone, managing associate at law firm Mishcon de Reya, told City AM.

“You only need to look at the residual effect on the wider global markets and the reports of the levels of US government involvement in this matter.”

Could it happen in the UK?

Unlike fellow Silicon Valley founders Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Huang does not hold special voting shares protecting him from being ousted.

Yet Nvidia’s directors reversed their decision less than a week after chairman Harvey Jones publicly ruled out Huang’s return.

Featherstone said Nvidia’s success appeared to have been dependent on Huang “without a huge amount of independent governance”.

He pointed to the greater emphasis placed on board independence in Britain, where the UK Corporate Governance Code provides that the roles of chief executive and chairman should be held by separate individuals.

Directors are also subject to statutory duties under the Companies Act 2006, including exercising independent judgement and avoiding conflicts of interest.

Lucinda Brendon, also of Mishcon de Reya, told City AM that allegations of personal or professional misconduct would ordinarily warrant a thorough investigation before a board determined its next steps.

“Absent a board demonstrating clear steps taken, it is difficult to shed the perception that governance has been overlooked,” she said.

Nvidia has established a new committee of independent directors to oversee overseas trade compliance and national security risks, alongside plans to appoint a chief compliance officer who will not report to Huang.

The board said it was confident Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk following input from senior US government officials.

However, Trump, who claimed he had “made the deal” to secure Huang’s return, could have personally gained as much as $15m from Monday’s rally, according to estimates based on his financial disclosures first reported by the Financial Times.

Democratic senators have since called for an investigation.

Can the AI rally hold?

Beyond supplying the chips powering the world’s leading AI models, Nvidia has become a major financier of the industry, investing billions of dollars in customers that in turn purchase its products.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said Huang’s return suggested Nvidia’s directors could not envisage a future for the company without him.

“We’ve had the Fed put, the Trump put, now we have the Jensen put to backstop the market when sell offs get brutal,” she said.

However, the broader pressures facing the AI industry remain, including rising borrowing costs, mounting infrastructure bills and uncertainty over investment returns.

The world’s largest cloud computing companies accounted for around 52 per cent of Nvidia’s revenue in its latest quarter, leaving the chipmaker exposed to any slowdown in data centre spending.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, warned the saga had exposed how far the risks associated with a single executive could spread.

“You might hold Nvidia through an index fund, own shares in a cloud company that buys its chips and invest in a utility supplying a data centre. On paper, those are three different investments. Next week, they could all react to the same news about one person,” she said.

Huang is due to face questioning from three congressional committees next week, while Nvidia’s internal investigation remains ongoing.

Investors are already tempering their enthusiasm, with Nvidia shares falling around six per cent in early trading on Tuesday.

articles.title: Tube strikes confirmed after last-ditch talks fail
articles.summary:
A series of strikes on the London Underground will go ahead on Thursday after last-ditch talks between Transport for London and the RMT union failed.

Union members are set to walk out from midday on Thursday, with further strikes planned on 17 and 19 December, 4 and 6 January, and 17, 23, and 25 February.

RMT said the 24-hour strike action by London Underground train drivers is set to go ahead due to a dispute over TFL plans to impose an optional four day work for train drivers.

The Union said it opposes the four-day working week despite the conditions being accepted by another transport union, Aslef.

From midday on Thursday, some London Underground services are expected to be running but there will be disruption across all lines. No service is expected on the Circle or Piccadilly lines throughout the day, or the Waterloo & City line after 12pm.

Talks between the RMT and TfL, which were held at the conciliation service, Acas, ended “after management refused to budge on demands that the union had put to the company consistently since March 2025 when the ‘offer’ was first made”, RMT said.

RMT, which announced the strike plans on 6 November, opposes the optional four-day working week.

“RMT has already suspended strike action three times for talks, yet no real improvements have been forthcoming,” RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said.

“There is nothing voluntary about a scheme that forces drivers to give up existing protections whether they work four days or five and threatens those who refuse with displacement from their depots,” he added.

Christmas party season set to be derailed

The City’s hospitality sector is set to be hit by the series of tube strikes, which begin during one of the busiest trading periods of the year.

The strikes threaten to disrupt Christmas parties across the capital as well as weekend shopping plans, dealing a blow to the hospitality sector during peak season.

On 18 November, Ed Richardson, transport programme director at advocacy group BusinessLDN, told City AM: “While many people will be able to work from home or use other modes of travel, it will hit the hospitality sector particularly hard during the vital Christmas trading season.”

articles.title: Anthropic loses $1 trillion crown as it sinks below IPO price
articles.summary:
Anthropic lost its $1 trillion market capitalisation on Tuesday after the firm’s shares dropped below their initial public offering price.

The Claude maker’s valuation surged to $2 trillion on its public market last week, but its valuation has since sunk to $998.2bn, as investors continue to rotate out of tech stocks following Monday’s blistering rally.

Anthropic’s shares tumbled 11.7 per cent to $77.3, taking the AI lab’s stock below its initial price offering of $83 for the first time since it started trading.

Since its debut market close, Anthropic has shed 20.7 per cent.

“The loss of the $83 IPO price is a major development, coming so swiftly after the listing. By comparison it was a month before SpaceX suffered the same fate,” said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG.

“Launching a major IPO in the midst of one of the biggest tech selloffs of recent times was never going to be great timing.”

Weighing on Anthropic’s future

Analysts added Anthropic’s fall from grace could further “sour demand” for AI-related stocks and overall sentiment towards the sector.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said: “Anthropic’s underwriters cannot defend this level, after they exercised their full option to buy the stock on November 20th. 

“This means that the current price action is based on pure investors sentiment towards Anthropic, which seems to be rapidly weakening.”

Brooks added the quick drop could “weigh on future earnings reports of its largest backers”, including Amazon and Alphabet, as it will affect “their bottom lines”.

Both Amazon and Alphabet have dipped 1.1 per cent, but losses “could worsen if Anthropic’s share price continues to decline”.

Huang’s return

Beauchamp added that Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia chief executive seems to “have amplified the instinct to sell” Anthropic shares, after his reinstatement sent Nvidia’s shares up over 31 per cent on Monday.

The chipmaker failed to extend its rally, shedding 8.6 per cent since Wall Street’s opening bell, while other firms also fell under selling pressure.

Intel and Micron lost 9.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent respectively.

The Nasdaq 100 also reentered the red, falling 2.6 per cent, keeping it well below its October peak. The S&P 500 slid 0.9 per cent.

articles.title: Mas and Magic can Conquer Coral Gold Cup contenders
articles.summary:
NEWBURY plays host to the Coral Gold Cup (3:00pm) which is the feature on a competitive card.

This year’s renewal looks a cracker, with Jamie Snowden’s Wendigo heading the betting.

His chance is hard to dispute. He was a ready winner at Carlisle last time and escapes a penalty. With some strong form in Grade One company, he looks certain to prove better than a mark of 147 in time.

However, he would prefer more cut in the ground, so at 4/1, I’m happy to look elsewhere.

Intriguingly, I think a Pertemps Qualifier over hurdles at this track holds the key to the race.

The winner that day was MASACCIO for Alan King.

Returning from a break since April 2025, the market suggested it was a pipe opener for future targets, with the nine-year-old sent off at 33/1, but he looked as good as ever, picking off his rivals up the straight.

That performance showed he retains plenty of ability, while his chase form is particularly strong, including several placed efforts behind subsequent King George winner The Jukebox Man and a third in the Plate behind Jagwar.

He looks well handicapped off 147 and can make up for lost time after missing this race last year through injury.

At 16/1, he makes great each-way appeal.

MIAMI MAGIC finished second to Masaccio in the aforementioned Pertemps Qualifier, so I don’t want to leave him alone either.

His chase mark of 145 could be lenient given it remains unchanged from April, when running a career-best before falling in the Grade One Mildmay at Aintree.

Still open to improvement as a seven-year-old, he looks well handicapped and with his latest outing hopefully blowing away the cobwebs from a wind-op over the summer, he looks overpriced at 11/1.

The Gerry Feilden (2:25pm) features short-priced favourite Idaho Sun, a Grade One winner who looks well treated off 142.

However, he has already been withdrawn on quicker ground this season, and with little rain forecast, his participation is far from certain.

LA CONQUIERE is the selection at around 8/1.

She was beaten a neck by Kateira last time, who has since won in Grade Two company, handles better ground and looks nicely weighted off 132.

The fourth and final selection comes in the preceding race, where COURT IN THE ACT catches the eye.

Harry Derham’s runner has been absent for over 600 days but boasts a strong record fresh and is one of the few currently jocked up.

With this contest likely to cut up, 14/1 is worth a small win-only bet.

Away from the track, on Monday 7th December at the Royal Lancaster Hotel in London, the racing industry will come together to celebrate the best work of racing journalists, broadcasters, and photographers, as well as honour leading jockeys, trainers, and owners.

Yet this year’s HWPA Derby Awards Lunch is about more than recognition, as the event will be run as a vital fundraiser for a friend of the press room, Marcus Townend, who suffered a life-altering accident last year. 

A Silent Auction to raise money for Marcus will run in the two weeks leading up to the HWPA Derby Awards and will conclude on Monday 7th December. Notable lots include a money-can’t-buy trip to Coolmore and Ballydoyle, Willie Mullins gallops morning and stable tour, and a signed Harry Kane England shirt.

Silent auction fundraiser for Marcus Townend: https://thesilent.auction/e/hw

Just Giving page for Marcus Townend: https://www.justgiving.com/crowdfunding/marcustownend

Miami Magic e/w                           3.00pm                Newbury
Masaccio e/w                                 3.00pm                Newbury

articles.title: Ace and Away make for a Golden day at Gosforth Park
articles.summary:
THERE is Grade One action up north in the Fighting Fifth Hurdle (2.00pm) at Newcastle.

While it’s a Grade One in its own right, this race has a long-standing reputation as a Champion Hurdle trial, and Alexei and Mydaddypaddy look set to exhibit their Cheltenham claims at the highest level.

Alexei progressed well through last season, winning a Grade Two before finishing fourth in the Champion Hurdle and third in the Aintree Hurdle.

Mydaddypaddy on the other hand is the unexposed second-season hurdler with bucket loads of potential.

I can see why they’re vying for favouritism, but they seem short enough for me when you’ve got the defending champion in the field at a much bigger price.

GOLDEN ACE crashed the party last year at 22/1 and it’s hard to let her go off unbacked again.

She gets seven pounds off the geldings, which brings her to within a pound of Alexei and four pounds ahead of Mydaddypaddy on official ratings.

Unlike the boys, she has won twice at the top level too. 

She travelled well on her comeback before finishing third behind a smart rival, and with that under her belt, I think she’s primed for another big effort.

The 5/1 looks way too big, especially with Alexei heading the betting at just 6/4.

APPLE AWAY also looks worth a bet at Gosforth Park.

The Old Gold Racing mare contests the Rehearsal Handicap Chase (1.25pm) and I was encouraged by her reappearance at Carlisle.

That was over a trip too sharp, but she still showed plenty of zest to finish second.

She will relish the step up to three miles and I think her Grade One-winning back-class makes her terrific value at 10/1 each-way in a race which could cut up.

POINTERS                                       SATURDAY

Apple Away e/w                             1.25pm                 Newcastle

Golden Ace                                     2.00pm                 Newcastle

articles.title: Government backs British defence AI startup in $70m funding round
articles.summary:
The government has backed British defence tech startup Agon in a $70m (£53.7m) funding round, as ministers seek to reduce the UK’s reliance on overseas military technology.

The Series A round, which values the London-based company at $450m, marks the first joint investment by the government’s Sovereign AI Fund and National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF).

The round was led by venture capital firm Northzone, alongside existing investors Lakestar, Lux Capital and XYZ. Former Sequoia Capital boss Roelof Botha also joined as an investor.

Founded in January by former British Army officer Tristam Constant and Cambridge Aerospace co-founder Junaid Hussain, Agon develops software to train and test autonomous military systems.

The company is building what it describes as a “virtual battlefield”, allowing defence companies to test AI-powered systems in simulated environments rather than relying on costly physical trials.

The latest investment brings Agon’s total funding to $100m, following a $30m seed round earlier this year.

The company, which has offices in London and Berlin, will use the funding to expand its engineering and research teams and grow its work with government and defence industry customers.

“Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare,” Constant said.

Hussain added: “Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend.”

Ramping up sovereign AI investment

The investment follows an additional £140m commitment to the Sovereign AI Fund at last month’s Budget, alongside an expansion of its remit to cover robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

The fund typically makes equity investments of between £1m and £10m in early-stage and growing British AI companies, although the size of the government’s investment in Agon has not been disclosed.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era.”

“But not only that, Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure these technologies are reliable, trustworthy, and deployed responsibly.”

The funding comes amid a surge in investor appetite for European defence tech companies as governments ramp up military spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

European defence tech startups attracted a record $7.4bn in investment this year by October, according to figures from Dealroom and Resilience Media.

Agon co-founder Hussain’s other defence venture, Cambridge Aerospace, secured a $3.4bn valuation in August, while German defence technology firm Stark Defence has raised €500m.

A spokesperson for NSSIF said the investment demonstrated how government-backed funds could work together to “accelerate strategically important technologies” and help British companies grow.

articles.title: Poundland bidder Xyra clinches funding and plots expansion of retailer
articles.summary:
One of the frontrunners to buy Poundland has now secured full funding for its bid and is plotting to expand the discount retailer’s store footprint if it succeeds in a takeover, City AM has learned. 

Xyra Group Holdings, whose bid is being led by former BHS boss Tony Brown, will also ask the firm to extend a notice to appoint administrators to allow it to conduct due diligence, meaning the struggling retailer could face a further period in limbo.

Poundland is due to collapse into administration in the early hours of Thursday, when a notice to appoint administrators comes into effect, meaning the high street giant would likely be broken apart. 

Xyra is among four bidders racing to take over Poundland before then, alongside Irish car park-owner Martin Property Group, German investment firm Zachert Private Equity and Dubai-based wholesaler Premier Quality Foods.

Speaking publicly about Xyra’s bid for the first time, Brown told City AM: “Pending customary due diligence by identified lenders and investors, Xyra has secured interest to cover the required funding to complete the acquisition of Poundland as a going concern.” 

The little-known investment firm has presented Gordon Brothers, Poundland’s owner, with plans to widen Poundland’s estate, which currently stands at about 600 sites, by taking up new shops in areas of the UK where the investment firm believes the retailer is currently underrepresented.

Brown’s plan to boost the retailer’s performance would see the high street giant widen its number of exclusive ranges – in products like toiletries and fashion accessories – in a bid to fatten its margins, sources with knowledge of the matter told City AM.

The notice to appoint administrators, filed by Poundland’s management, blocked creditors from calling in their debts for an initial 10-day period. This was then extended and will lapse at midnight on Wednesday.

Sources close to the process had previously said there would be a “very high bar” for extending this moratorium a second time, but it is understood that Xyra Group would request this extra time for its financial backers to complete their due diligence.

Brown said: “Xyra will ask the seller for a short period of exclusivity and remains committed to its bid, which will preserve Poundland’s stores, its colleagues and its place on the high street.”

This extension would need to be triggered by Poundland’s management, who would have to apply to the courts for this to be approved. 

Poundland’s directors would be able to extend this deadline if Gordon Brothers reassured the retailer it would have access to the funds it needs to make it through these extra 10 days, people with knowledge of the discussions told City AM.

Poundland bidder plots more stores

The discount retailer has tussled with Gordon Brothers in recent weeks over claims the investment firm had been restricting its access to vital funds needed to pay suppliers and staff.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, said earlier this month he had seen evidence that Poundland was being “strangled of access” to its own cash.

Gordon Brothers made two payments of about £10m each to Poundland earlier this month and is expected to release funds needed to cover the pay of the retailer’s near-12,000 staff this week.

Xyra Group Holdings is an investment vehicle led by 23-year-old entrepreneur Manvedeep Singh. The group has never previously completed an acquisition but has called upon a number of City veterans in its attempts to get its bid over the line. 

Brown, who is fronting Xyra’s bid for Poundland, has held leadership roles at retailers including Beales, BHS and Peacocks. 

A sticking point of Gordon Brothers’s attempted sale of Poundland has been its insistence that bidders cover at least part of a loan attached to the retailer, of which it holds £22.5m. Xyra has offered to pay £12.5m of this up front.

Gordon Brothers declined to comment.

articles.title: Tech stocks slide as Nvidia rally loses steam
articles.summary:
Tech stocks across Wall Street slid on Tuesday as investors pulled back from AI-linked companies following the Nvidia-fuelled rally that delivered one of the strongest trading sessions in months.

The Nasdaq Composite fell as much as 1.7 per cent in early trading before paring its losses to around 1.1 per cent, trading at 23,835 points, while the S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent to 7,206.

Nvidia shares dropped around six per cent after the opening bell, reversing some of Monday’s 31.4 per cent surge, which restored nearly $1 trillion to the chipmaker’s market value following Jensen Huang’s surprise reinstatement as chief executive.

Other chipmakers came under pressure ahead of the opening bell, with Micron shedding more than six per cent, while AMD and Broadcom fell five per cent and four per cent respectively.

The renewed sell-off comes after the Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5 per cent higher on Monday, its 23rd biggest daily percentage gain since its inception in 1971, while the S&P 500 gained 4.7 per cent.

However, the Nasdaq remains well below its October peak, with concerns over rising interest rates, stretched technology valuations and the sustainability of AI spending continuing to weigh on investors.

Markets are also awaiting US inflation figures later this week for further indications of the Federal Reserve’s next move ahead of its December meeting.

Nvidia scrutiny continues

Huang’s reinstatement has eased some concerns over Nvidia’s leadership, but the chipmaker continues to face scrutiny over its corporate governance and financing of the wider AI industry.

His return came after Donald Trump intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board to reinstate its co-founder, less than a fortnight after he resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Trump could have personally gained as much as $15m from Monday’s Nvidia rally, according to estimates based on his financial disclosures first reported by the Financial Times, prompting Democratic senators to call for an investigation.

Nvidia is also facing forthcoming Congressional hearings and an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission into its accounting practices.

Spending by the world’s largest cloud computing companies is forecast to reach $1 trillion this year, rising to $1.4 trillion next year, according to figures cited by AJ Bell.

Tuesday’s losses on Wall Street contrasted with a stronger session across Asian markets, where South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 closed 3.9 per cent higher as chipmakers benefited from Monday’s US rally.

articles.title: UK firms warned on hiring workers abroad amid Russia and North Korea threat
articles.summary:
British firms have been warned about the security risks of hiring remote IT workers as the Treasury said paid work could lead to the funds being passed to North Korea and Russia. 

In a lengthy report on the financial risks facing businesses and various industries, the Treasury warned that firms risked financing hostile actors including North Korea. 

An update on national financial risks since the last report in 2021 states that remote employment of IT workers left UK firms exposed to sanctions risks. 

The Treasury’s latest assessment of proliferation financing, which is where funds or financial services support the development of destructive weapons such as nuclear arms or bio weapons, suggested that remote employment was a “cross-cutting” risk for firms across all sectors. 

North Korean workers use online freelance platforms and VPNs in order to conceal their true location, according to government officials. It means that the remote employment of IT workers could lead to funds being transferred to the country, which faces several sanctions by the UK and US, or sensitive data being shared. 

The report also warned that several North Korean nationals lived in Russia, raising the threat regarding money laundering and large-scale financial thefts. The Treasury said that the convergence of relations between Russia, North Korea and Iran through partnerships made the web of financing more hazardous for firms given sanctions could be bypassed. 

Firms’ reliance on digital services and declining levels of visibility over workers’ identities or payment flows made the UK more vulnerable. 

City minister Lucy Rigby said the UK’s status as a global financial hub “inherently exposes us to risk”. 

North Korea and Russia’s security threats

Last year, City AM reported on the rise of remote hiring practices among British firms, which looked to reduce tax burdens after a £25bn hike on employers’ National Insurance contributions. 

North Korea was recently accused of being behind a record £4.7bn hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. 

The FBI said the attack was conducted by state-backed hacking group Tradertraitor. 

According to research in the Lowy Institute, a security think tank, state authorities take nearly all of the income generated by North Korean workers living abroad. Its report said that overseas labourers made up to an estimated $800m for the regime. Between 80 and 90 per cent of workers’ earnings are reportedly directed to the state or affiliated organisations.

Neil Carberry, chief executive of the CIPD, the industry body for human resources, said: “It’s a mistake for firms to cut costs on hiring in ways that forget that who you have in your business is at the heart of service and security. Understanding who new hires are, their skills and motivation – and even their humanity – is critical.”

articles.title: Senegal reinstated as Afcon champions after winning CAS appeal over walk-off
articles.summary:
Senegal have been reinstated as reigning champions of the Africa Cup of Nations after winning an appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

The independent panel sided with the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) over its challenge to being stripped of the title in March by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

CAF had awarded the crown to Morocco after deeming Senegal to have forfeited the final by walking off the pitch for 14 minutes in protest at a penalty award late in the game, which they won 1-0 in January.

“After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee’s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority,” CAS said in a statement.

“By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.”

CAS added: “The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as ‘arbitrary’. On the contrary, the Referee’s judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.”

How the Afcon final walk-off led to Senegal losing the title

The dispute rested on CAF’s interpretation of the Afcon rulebook. While Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon regulations state that walking off the pitch without authorisation should trigger a forfeiture, CAS that only applied in the event of the game being called off.

The FSF cited Fifa’s Laws of the Game, which say that the referee’s decision is final, and CAS agreed with that position.

The decision comes as a blow to Morocco, an increasingly influential Fifa member and co-host of the men’s World Cup in 2030, and CAF.

Senegal’s victory in the final in Rabat was an upset for the hosts and capped a chaotic and hugely contentious conclusion to the tournament.

Their players staged a walk-off when Morocco were awarded a penalty, only for Brahim Diaz to miss the spot-kick when play eventually resumed. The match went to extra time and Pape Gueye scored the only goal in the 94th minute.

CAF initially fined and suspended individual players and officials from both sides but upheld the result, yet a further appeal from Moroccan football authorities led to CAF overturning that decision and awarding Morocco a 3-0 win – and the trophy.

articles.title: ‘Act now’: MI5 urges defence firms to ramp up security amid Russia threat
articles.summary:
Britain’s intelligence service has urged firms providing support to Ukraine’s military to “act now” to defend themselves from the rising threat of Russian sabotage.

A joint alert by the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the organisation that runs MI5’s security mission warned Russia was ramping up “attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence-related facilities”. Companies should clamp down on avenues through which Russian actors can “conduct hostile reconnaissance, and attack people, sites or operations”, they added.

“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target,” the MoD and National Protective Security Authority (NPSA) wrote, in what is the first time MI5 has directly accused Russia of wrongdoing. “This includes organisations in the supply chain.”

They added that Russia’s attempts to sabotage European defence-related facilities was “typically characterised by the use of proxy actors, employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson”.

British defence firms tied to Ukraine

Almost all Britain’s largest defence companies have in some way helped arm Ukraine’s military in its years-long war against Russia. Last week, Northern Ireland’s Thales provided over 1,000 short-range air defence missiles to the front line as part of the UK’s £240m winter support programme signed off by the MoD.

Majors including BAE Systems, Babcock and Qinetiq have also helped directly or via supply chains throughout much of the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.

Western adminsitrations have accused Russia of waging a hybrid war effort against Europe, after a string of cyber and guerrilla attacks on the region. Earlier this year, a Moscow-linked cell was held responsible for arson incidents on the home of then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

At the time, the Russian Embassy in London said it rejected “any attempt to associate Russia or its foreign ministry with unlawful activities”.

The alert published on Tuesday provides firms with a series of measures firms in the sector can take to minimise their exposure to any Russian sabotage efforts. Among them are steps to keep “unnecessary public information” to a minimum and adopt a “security-minded approach to communications and online activity”.

Bosses were also told to educate staff on how to recognise “hostile reconnaissance, and protect their personal security.

Louise Sandher-Jones, the armed forces minister, said: “Britain’s adversaries are not limiting themselves to military targets. They are prepared to use cyberattacks, espionage, sabotage and hostile reconnaissance against the companies, technology and supply chains that underpin our national security.”
