articles.title: How skipping breakfast to save room for dinner shocks your blood sugar and metabolism
articles.summary:
Fasting all morning to save room for a big holiday feast might seem like a smart strategy, but experts say it can have unwanted health effects, and that there are better ways to prepare.

When people go hours without food, blood sugar levels drop, triggering headaches, nausea and irritability, according to Gabrielle Kishner, a registered dietitian nutritionist and founder in New York City.

"Once we get those uncomfortable symptoms of hunger, we're going to eat really fast when we get into Thanksgiving, because we're starving," Kishner told Fox News Digital. "We're also going to crave more carbs and sugar to get that blood sugar back up."

DOCTORS SETTLE DEBATE OVER DRINKING COFFEE ON AN EMPTY STOMACH AND POTENTIAL HEALTH RISKS

Previous research has found that skipping daytime meals leads to significantly higher post-meal blood glucose spikes at dinner compared with eating regular meals.

Regular breakfast omission has also been linked to disrupted circadian rhythms, impaired insulin sensitivity and a sluggish metabolism, as well as compensatory eating later in the day.

To avoid coming to the dinner table starving, Kishner recommends eating a balanced breakfast within two hours of waking up and avoiding gaps of longer than four to six hours without food.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Combining carbohydrates, protein, fiber and healthy fats like Greek yogurt with berries and chia seeds, or avocado toast topped with hard-boiled eggs, helps stabilize energy and blood sugar, so diners arrive "comfortably hungry," she said.

If the main meal takes place early in the afternoon, a balanced midmorning snack containing two nutrient groups, like vegetables and hummus, can help bridge the gap.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

How diners build that first plate also affects digestion and energy.

Kishner recommends filling half the plate with fiber-rich fruits and vegetables, eating those first to slow digestion and help stabilize fullness.

The second half of the plate should be split evenly between protein, like turkey, and carbohydrates, such as stuffing or mashed potatoes.

Once the meal begins, pacing plays a major role in preventing gastrointestinal distress, Kishner said. Eating quickly makes it harder for the stomach to break down poorly chewed food, leading to bloating and discomfort.

It takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes for the stomach to send satiety signals to the brain, meaning fast eaters often consume far more food than they need before realizing they are full, according to Cleveland Clinic.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Kishner recommends pausing midway through the meal to assess hunger levels, and waiting 10 to 20 minutes after finishing a plate before going back for seconds.

Rich, creamy and sugary dishes take longer to digest, so sampling small portions from the dessert table helps to prevent stomachaches without making favorite foods off-limits.

For those who do end up overindulging, gentle movement afterward can ease the post-meal slump. Kishner suggests taking a 10- to 15-minute walk with family or friends after the meal to aid digestion and blood sugar regulation.

Blood sugar typically peaks 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, and even brief, light-intensity walking helps blunt glucose spikes and keep insulin levels steady. Drinking water throughout the day also helps to digest food, according to Kishner.

Above all, Kishner urges diners not to compensate the next morning by restricting food or skipping breakfast again, which only restarts the cycle of blood sugar crashes and overeating.

articles.title: Trump administration weighs targeting Iran's top regime leaders in bid to end war: report
articles.summary:
The Trump administration has renewed internal discussions about potentially targeting senior Iranian regime leaders in strikes that some officials believe could end the ongoing war, according to reports.

Citing a U. S. official and another source, NBC News reported Tuesday that some officials believe eliminating senior figures could pressure Tehran to end the conflict by showing that Washington can locate and strike the regime's leadership at any time.

Though the option has long been under consideration, it has "been under renewed discussion in recent weeks" as President Donald Trump deliberates over the next phase of the war, two sources told the outlet.

The deliberations come amid reports that Iran could be developing a radioactive "dirty bomb" and a report citing U. S. intelligence assessments of potential Iranian plots involving chemical weapons aimed at senior officials in Washington.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN ABOUT REPORTED PLOT AGAINST ADMIN OFFICIALS: 'WE TAKE IT VERY SERIOUSLY'

"We know a lot about what's happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We'll find out about it. We will not allow that," Trump had told reporters at the White House Nov. 20.

Iran's surviving leadership includes Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, after the elder Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes of the war Feb. 28.

Other senior figures in Iran's military and national security apparatus include Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Commander Ahmad Vahidi, armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Mohsen Rezaei, a former IRGC commander in chief reportedly appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council in August 2026.

AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS

NBC News did not identify any of those officials as specific targets of the operations under discussion.

Administration officials opposed to the proposal have reportedly warned that targeting Iranian leaders could expose American officials to retaliatory attacks, stiffen the resolve of surviving regime figures and undermine future diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, now in its ninth month. 

The administration continues to weigh military options, enforce its naval blockade and assert control over the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

The debate comes months after U. S. and Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader and other senior military and intelligence officials, igniting a prolonged conflict centered on Tehran's nuclear program, ballistic missile capabilities and regional military activities.

Mojtaba Khamenei, who was reportedly injured in the strikes that killed his father, has not been seen publicly since assuming power, though he has warned Washington and Jerusalem against resuming major attacks on Iranian leadership.

MOJTABA KHAMENEI DEFIES ‘MALICIOUS’ ATTACKS AS US ARMY ZEROES IN ON IRAN’S 350,000 TROOPS

"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," a statement attributed to Khamenei said.

The warning reportedly followed a meeting with senior Iranian military commanders, including Abdollahi, Hatami and Vahidi. On Oct. 31, Khamenei also directed Iran's armed forces to prepare an "immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response" to any future threats.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing," a White House official told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

"The president has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Task Force Iron Gate will continue with full effect. 

"President Trump has many options at his disposal and will make the best possible decision to ensure Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon. "

articles.title: Iran to execute 2 anti-regime protesters at dawn after 3 days in death row holding cells
articles.summary:
Two Iranian anti-regime protesters face execution within hours after spending three days in pre-execution holding cells at Ghezel Hesar Prison, according to a human rights organization warning that the men were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and unfair trials.

Milad Armoun, 27, and Navid Najaran, 34, are scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO).

The men were transferred to solitary confinement on Nov. 21 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld their death sentences.

IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE

Both men were arrested during Iran's 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" uprising and are defendants in the high-profile "Ekbatan case," which stems from the killing of a member of Iran's Basij paramilitary force during nationwide anti-government demonstrations.

Exiled Iranian crown prince Reza Phahlavi said on X on Tuesday that the execution would take place at dawn.

IRANIAN REGIME CRITIC WARNS TRUMP DEAL COULD BE 'LIFELINE' FOR REGIME, CLAIMS PEOPLE ARE 'NERVOUS'

"Despite being acquitted of the murder charge, Milad Armon and Navid Najjaran have been sentenced to death by "hanging judge" Abolqasem Salavati.

"The execution orders for these two political prisoners have been sent to their lawyers, to be carried out at dawn on Wednesday, Azar 4."

"Milad and Navid were held in Ward 33 which houses those accused of murder before being transferred to solitary confinement in preparation for their executions today," a source told IHRNGO.

The men were sentenced to death in May by Branch 15 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, on charges of efsad-fil-arz , or "corruption on earth," a capital offense under Iranian law.

Salavati has faced longstanding criticism from human rights organizations over his handling of political cases and the harsh sentences imposed on government opponents.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, condemned the sentences and called for immediate international intervention.

"Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and grossly unfair trials. Their executions would be an irreversible injustice and another example of the Islamic Republic’s use of the death penalty as a tool of political repression.

IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS

"Strong international reactions may be the only way to save their lives. We urge the UN and all governments with diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic to intervene immediately to stop their executions," Amiry-Moghaddam said in a statement.

The Ekbatan case centers on the death of Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Aliverdi was injured during unrest in Tehran's Ekbatan neighborhood in 2022, and died two days later. Iranian authorities accused several protesters of involvement in his death.

Armoun was arrested in Tehran in November 2022, while Najaran was detained the following month in Ahvaz.

Iran Human Rights alleged that both men were tortured and subjected to ill-treatment to obtain self-incriminating confessions subsequently broadcast by Iranian state media.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Defense attorneys also accused judicial authorities of barring lawyers from hearings, withholding case documents and obstructing appeals.

Earlier death sentences tied to murder charges were overturned, and Najaran was acquitted of involvement in the killing in a separate proceeding. However, the Revolutionary Court subsequently imposed death sentences under Iran's national security laws.

The death sentences of two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, were overturned, and their cases referred for retrial, according to human rights organizations.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman detained by morality police over allegations that she improperly wore her hijab.

The demonstrations spread nationwide, becoming one of the most significant challenges to Iran's clerical leadership in decades.

articles.title: FDA approves first new breast cancer hormone therapy in over two decades
articles.summary:
A new early-stage breast cancer therapy has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration for the first time in more than two decades.

Wilserdly (giredestrant), an oral hormone therapy from San Francisco-based drugmaker Genentech, received the approval after positive trial results in treating adults with early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer.

This subtype is the most common form of the disease in which tumor growth is fueled by the hormone estrogen rather than excess levels of the HER2 protein.

NEW DRUG APPROACH OFFERS HOPE FOR PATIENTS WITH RECURRENT AGGRESSIVE CANCERS

The Phase 3 lidERA study showed that the drug reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 30% compared to standard endocrine therapy, including generic pharmaceuticals like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors, according to a Genentech press release.

Patients were also less likely to quit treatment because of side effects like joint pain and hot flashes compared to standard options, the researchers noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The study found a reduction in cancer returning in distant parts of the body, like the bones, liver or lungs.

Aditya Bardia, M.D., global principal investigator of the lidERA breast cancer trial and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, noted that this finding is "particularly significant" because once breast cancer spreads to distant organs, it is "generally no longer curable."

The foundational hormone therapies used for early-stage breast cancer have remained "largely unchanged" since the 2000s, Bardia told Fox News Digital.

"These medicines have saved countless lives, but there has been room for improvement, both in terms of effectiveness and tolerability," he said.

"Now, for the first time in more than two decades, we have a new foundational hormone treatment that has been shown to be more effective than our existing standard therapies in early-stage breast cancer."

Because most breast cancers are caught early and fall into the hormone receptor-positive subtype, the new therapy has the potential to help a large number of patients, Bardia added.

Earlier this year, the FDA also approved Wilserdly combined with everolimus, an oral cancer medication, for the treatment of adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer whose disease had recurred during or after completing endocrine-based therapy.

This makes Wilserdly the "first and only" SERD (selective estrogen receptor degrader) that is FDA-approved to treat both early-stage and advanced ER-positive breast cancer.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Levi Garraway, M.D., chief medical officer and head of global product development, commented in a statement that the FDA approval is due to the drug showing "superior efficacy" against other therapies that have long been the standard of care.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, plans to continue investing in "broad development" of Wilserdly, exploring its potential across disease stages and in new treatment combinations, according to Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham.

Bardia encouraged patients to speak with their oncologists about the new treatment option, particularly those whose recent diagnosis is "consistent with the regulatory label and approval of the drug. "

articles.title: Vatican releases Pope Francis' private diary detailing spiritual crisis, encounters with the devil
articles.summary:
Excerpts from the late Pope Francis' private diary published Tuesday reveal that the pontiff endured a two-year spiritual crisis beginning in 2021, writing that he felt tempted by the devil and struggled with the weight of wielding power over the Catholic Church.

The 160-page volume, "The Private Diary of Pope Francis," was compiled by Cardinal Victor Fernandez and spans entries from December 1992 through August 2024 — eight months before Francis died in April 2025 at age 88 — marking the first papal diary made public since the 1960s.

In a December 2022 entry, Francis described his crisis as "all mixed with governance issues, pressure regarding decisions to make, and aridity and desolation," adding that he resisted becoming a leader "who uses others like puppets."

MYSTERIOUS BLOOD-SOAKED RELIC LINKED TO HISTORY'S MOST BELOVED SAINT, ST. FRANCIS OF ASSISI, GOES ON DISPLAY

Across the entries, Francis wrote that he believed he had seen the devil three times — including during a Vatican meeting — and recalled a June 2018 vision of hell.

"Last night I saw the entrance to Hell," he wrote in the 2018 entry. "I peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon. I thank the Lord for this help."

Reacting Tuesday on "Varney & Co.," Fox News contributor and theologian Jonathan Morris said he was most struck not by the late pope's spiritual struggles, but by the Vatican's decision to publish them.

POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL

"I think the most surprising part is that this was actually published, not so much that it happened, " Morris said. "Spiritual warfare is a very basic Christian doctrine, and even the last things — death, judgment, heaven, hell. And apparently he saw the gates of hell. Those are the core beliefs of the church across all sorts of denominations within Christianity."

Morris added that Francis' successor, Pope Leo XIV — whom Francis praised in the diary as "a great pastor, a generous missionary, and an irreproachable man" — approved releasing the writings so they might help others facing similar trials.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel raises prospect of preemptive strike over emerging Iranian chemical weapons threat
articles.summary:
Israel accused Iran of developing chemical weapons Tuesday and raised the possibility of a preemptive strike to prevent Tehran from using them, warning that the regime seeks a strategic advantage after major setbacks in its war with Israel and the United States.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz told reporters in Tel Aviv that Israel and the U.S. have intelligence indicating Iran began developing chemical weapons after their joint military campaign launched Feb. 28.

Katz declined to disclose how far the program has progressed or where the weapons are being developed, though he noted Israeli intelligence has monitored Iran's effort for months and said that operational plans are in place.

BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said, according to Israel's i24NEWS.

"This intelligence information reached both the United States and Israel," he said.

"Israel is determined not to allow Iran to acquire this kind of chemical weapons capability that would threaten the country and the entire region," he added.

Katz described the program as a potentially game-changing threat to Israel and the broader Middle East, warning that the weapons could give Tehran leverage to rebuild its depleted military infrastructure, including its nuclear program.

LIVE WWII-ERA GRENADES TURN UP IN UNLIKELY PLACE; BOMB SQUAD WARNS OF DANGER

"They came out of the tunnels and saw what happened to them," Katz said of Iranian forces following the April ceasefire, according to comments reported by The Times of Israel.

"They are looking for a weapon that gives them some balance against us. This process in Iran is new and comes in the wake of the damage they suffered. True, it is not nuclear, but it is still unconventional weapons."

"If we thought this was already an unfolding event, we would act," Katz said.

Katz also said that Israel must maintain the ability to act preemptively if intelligence shows an Iranian attack is imminent.

"If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure," Katz said, according to Israel's Ynet news outlet.

ISRAEL’S LEADING CONTENDER FOR PRIME MINISTER CLASHES WITH NETANYAHU OVER IRAN STRIKES

The allegations come amid heightened U. S. intelligence concerns over Iranian threats against the American homeland.

CNN reported Nov. 16, citing seven U. S. officials, that American intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological "dirty bomb" or chemical weapon.

Sources familiar with the intelligence described the planning as an effort to preserve potential retaliatory options rather than evidence of an imminent strike.

The White House said at the time that it was monitoring potential threats but had identified no credible threats to the U.S. homeland.

President Donald Trump subsequently warned that Iran would face severe consequences if it carried out such an attack.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the reporting as "Iraq War-style propaganda" with "Israeli fingerprints all over it."

"Nobody is buying it," Araghchi wrote on X.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet cleared to shoot down Russian missile over Poland as Warsaw pushes for US troops
articles.summary:
Poland announced Tuesday it had renewed its push for a permanent U.S. military presence in the country after two Russian airspace incursions in four days, including one in which a Swedish fighter jet under NATO command was cleared to shoot down a Russian cruise missile but held its fire.

The latest incursion came overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during attacks on Ukraine, four days after three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles had crossed into Poland, prompting NATO to scramble fighter jets and bolster air defenses along its eastern flank.

Poland's chargé d'affaires in Washington, Bogdan Klich, said Tuesday that he briefed the White House National Security Council on the violations and renewed Warsaw's call to permanently station American troops in the NATO member country.

US URGES AMERICANS IN HISTORIC REGION TO STAY ALERT AFTER 'DANGEROUS' AIRSPACE INCIDENT

"Yesterday, I briefed the U.S. National Security Council on the violation of Polish airspace by Russian Kh-101 missiles and once again discussed the issue of the permanent deployment of U.S. troops in Poland," Klich wrote on X.

The new diplomatic push follows the incidents involving Russian assets and heightened concerns that Moscow's war in Ukraine will spill into NATO territory.

The Nov. 20 incursion involved a Swedish JAS 39 Gripen pilot operating under NATO command who was authorized to engage a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, according to Lt. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, commander of Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, as reported by The Kyiv Independent.

NATO's Combined Air Operations Centre in Uedem, Germany, issued conditional authorization to fire, but the pilot could not positively identify the object visually or through the aircraft's onboard electro-optical systems because of severe weather, Nowak said. No weapons were fired.

SUPERSONIC RUSSIAN JETS TRIGGER JOINT SCRAMBLE BY NATO ALLIES AMID PUTIN 'CLOWNS' JAB

Polish authorities monitored 11 potentially threatening aerial objects during the attack, three of which entered the country's airspace, according to Nowak.

The Swedish Armed Forces said its jets had tracked several unidentified objects over Poland during the mission, which lasted several hours under difficult weather conditions.

Polish F-16 fighter jets, a Swedish Saab 340 early warning aircraft, a Dutch aerial refueling aircraft and ground-based air defense systems were also supporting the operation.

Polish prosecutors confirmed Sunday that debris recovered at three locations belonged to Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, revising an initial military assessment that one of the objects might have been a drone, according to reports.

RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

Preliminary findings indicated the missiles were manufactured in October or November 2026 at a factory in Dubna in Russia's Moscow region, prosecutors said.

The second incursion happened overnight Nov. 24, when a Russian drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine during another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Polish forces tracked the unmanned aircraft and received authorization to shoot it down but did not fire after it changed course and headed east, citing potential risks to civilians and property on the ground.

Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said Polish authorities believed the violation was deliberate.

"It's hard to imagine this being a coincidence, so we assume it was an intentional act," Zalewski told RMF FM, according to Reuters.

After an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council on Monday, Nov. 23, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe went on to authorize the forward deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to Poland.

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

"All Allies stand in full solidarity with Poland. NATO remains united, ready, and committed to defending against any threat," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on X and as Warsaw summoned Russia's ambassador, according to Reuters.

In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said U.S. and Polish officials were working toward an agreement that could accommodate up to 10,000 American troops.

Roughly 7,000 U.S. troops were stationed in Poland on a rotational basis at the time while a permanent installation would expand Washington's military commitment along NATO's eastern flank.

"We want the kind of U.S. presence that would reassure us but not be threatening to Russia," Sikorski said during a Council on Foreign Relations event in New York, Bloomberg reported.

President Donald Trump has previously voiced his support for a permanent U.S. military base in Poland, although Washington has also reviewed American troop deployments across Europe.

articles.title: Popular actor says bladder cancer discovery followed one strange bathroom symptom
articles.summary:
For "Star Trek: The Next Generation" star Jonathan Frakes, a life-altering health scare began not with physical pain, but with a strange sighting during a regular trip to Phoenix.

"My pee was pink," Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast, "Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny," alongside his co-star Brent Spiner and urologic surgeon Dr. Ram Narayanan. "I was unnerved."

Searching for an easy explanation, Frakes said he considered blaming his diet. Maybe it was beets, he mused, before realizing he hadn't touched one in six years.

MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS

Frakes ultimately called his doctor, a decision that may have saved his bladder.

According to Narayanan, Frakes experienced what is clinically known as painless gross hematuria, or visible blood in the urine without accompanying pain.

"When it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag," the doctor said on the podcast.

While blood in the urine can stem from benign causes like urinary tract infections or kidney stones, painless visible hematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. It always warrants an immediate urological evaluation, according to both Cleveland Clinic and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

DIAGNOSTIC TEST COULD FLAG WHICH MEN NEED AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER TREATMENT AND WHICH DON'T

Days after finishing a fan convention, Frakes underwent an in-office cystoscopy, a quick procedure in which a thin camera examines the lining of the bladder. Inside, Narayanan spotted small, fern-like growths.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Three days later, Frakes was in the operating room to undergo a blue light cystoscopy — a specialized exam that uses an imaging dye to make hidden tumors glow — and tumor resection to scrape away the abnormal tissue.

The biopsy confirmed high-grade, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

To illustrate why early timing was so critical, Narayanan compared the bladder to a layer cake — scraping away the surface "icing" removed the tumor before it could invade the deeper muscle wall, which often forces surgeons to remove the entire bladder and fashion a new one from a piece of intestine.

"At the end of it, he says, 'I think we got it all,'" Frakes recalled.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

To prevent the cancer from returning, Frakes underwent six weekly rounds of intravesical therapy, where a liquid medication is placed directly into the bladder.

While immunotherapy is the standard first-line treatment, a nationwide shortage led Narayanan to administer a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and docetaxel.

According to medical experts, this dual-agent chemotherapy has proven to be a highly effective alternative during immunotherapy shortages.

While inspecting Frakes’ bladder, Narayanan noticed a secondary issue: an enlarged prostate. As Frakes joked on air, his surgeon told him, "While I was in there, I noticed your prostate is the size of a small town."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The enlarged prostate was forcing Frakes’ bladder muscle to work overtime, a condition called trabeculation, which can eventually lead to bladder failure.

After ruling out prostate cancer via MRI, Narayanan performed a surgery to remove roughly 135 grams of obstructing tissue through a single tiny incision.

As a result, Frakes was able to stop taking his daily prostate medications, and his urinary symptoms vanished.

Other than immediate family, the actor kept his diagnosis private until deciding to share his story during Men’s Health Awareness Month to encourage other men to overcome their reluctance to see a urologist, whom Narayanan affectionately calls "primary care doctors below the belt."

"If something happens like [what] happened to you, check it out immediately," the doctor urged listeners. "Don't be shy. Don't be afraid."

articles.title: European leader warns Russian aggression could escalate within weeks or months
articles.summary:
Russia is growing increasingly willing to take risks against NATO countries, with a mounting campaign of sabotage, arson attacks and assassination plots that could escalate within weeks or months, Latvia’s president warned in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Western leaders may be underestimating the threat posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin because they fail to fully understand the ideological and historical beliefs driving the Kremlin’s foreign policy.

"The appetite for the risk is growing in Russia," Rinkēvičs said. "We see numbers of arson attacks. Some assassination plots. Acts of sabotage."

BATTLE-TESTED ZELENSKYY SOUNDS CHILLING ALARM ON WHERE PUTIN’S WAR COULD HEAD NEXT

While Russian provocations have so far remained below the threshold that would trigger NATO’s collective defense mechanism under Article 5, Rinkēvičs warned that the situation could deteriorate rapidly.

"We see that the number of attacks is rising, but we still see that, at this point, it may change very quickly. It may change maybe in weeks or months or a couple of months' time," he said.

The Latvian leader pointed to recent cooperation between Latvian and Estonian intelligence services that he said resulted in arrests in Estonia and prevented an attack against a defense factory.

He said the escalating campaign is part of Moscow’s strategy to discourage European countries from continuing to support Ukraine.

DENMARK ACCUSES RUSSIA OF PLOTTING TO KILL UKRAINIAN AMERICAN RAPPER ON DANISH SOIL

His warning comes just days after President Donald Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 19, for unprecedented talks that addressed the war in Ukraine and nuclear arms control.

On Monday, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Ukraine and NATO countries had already created circumstances in which Moscow could contemplate using nuclear weapons.

Medvedev also raised the possibility of a preemptive nuclear strike if Western countries supplied Ukraine with nuclear weapons, while acknowledging that Russia’s nuclear doctrine does not explicitly provide for preventive strikes, Anadolu reported.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Rinkēvičs argued that Western governments need to reconsider how they interpret Putin’s motivations, suggesting that conventional military, economic and political calculations alone cannot explain the Kremlin’s determination to continue the war.

"We are too pragmatic and rational in the West," he said.

The Latvian president pointed to Putin’s recent interviews, saying he was struck by the Russian leader’s ideological and religious references, including the historical concept of Russia as the "Third Rome" and its perceived mission to safeguard Christianity.

"I think that this kind of belief also drives the war," Rinkēvičs said, describing a "missionary approach that we in the West do not understand because we are too rational and too pragmatic."

While Rinkēvičs welcomed continued engagement between Washington and Moscow, he said last week’s summit had not produced a diplomatic breakthrough on Ukraine. 

"Russia is not willing to end this war," he said.

He argued that Moscow is using diplomatic engagement to extend the conflict in the hope of securing further gains both militarily and at the negotiating table.

Rinkēvičs said the combination of Russian ideological ambitions, escalating operations against Western countries, upcoming European elections in France, Poland and Italy and political debates in the U.S. could encourage Moscow to continue the fighting.

ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

The Latvian State Security Service confirmed that eight Latvian nationals were detained in Estonia on Nov. 14, after authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack against Threod Systems, an Estonian drone manufacturer.

Estonian security officials attributed the operation to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU.

Estonia subsequently announced it would close its land border with Russia beginning Dec. 1, for at least six months. Russia’s Foreign Ministry responded Monday by accusing Estonia of hostile actions "on the verge of triggering open war," Reuters reported.

British security officials also warned Tuesday that companies supporting Ukraine’s military should prepare for potential Russian sabotage attempts after a series of incidents across Europe, The Associated Press reported.

The Kremlin has consistently denied conducting sabotage operations against NATO countries.

As Fox News Digital reported Monday, new Western intelligence assessments suggest Russia could launch a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon within weeks, potentially threatening thousands of satellites used by the U.S. and its allies.

Rinkēvičs said he could not confirm the intelligence assessments but warned that Russia’s pursuit of advanced weapons requires greater Western investment in missile defenses, drones and emerging technologies.

"Russia is developing nuclear weapons, developing new technologies and we have to be extremely, extremely careful," he said.

However, he cautioned that Moscow has previously overstated its military capabilities.

"Whether that weapon in space, nuclear weapon in space is going to be the real thing or just a kind of fake news, remains to be seen," he said.

Despite his warnings, Rinkēvičs said an opportunity for meaningful negotiations could emerge next spring or summer if Ukraine withstands Russia’s winter offensive against its civilian and energy infrastructure.

"I'm quite confident Ukraine is going to survive. Unfortunately, the big question is at what human cost," he said.

Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting on Ukraine Monday, Rinkēvičs said Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure had reached their highest level since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.

He warned that millions of Ukrainians face the prospect of spending the winter without electricity, heating or running water.

"Winter must never be a weapon of war," he told the council.

Rinkēvičs also praised the Oleshky ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump as evidence that diplomatic pressure and political will can produce results.

For now, however, he remains skeptical that Moscow is genuinely seeking peace.

"Currently, Russia explores diplomatic efforts in order to prolong the war, not to end the war," he told Fox News Digital.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this article.

articles.title: What United Airlines banning AI agents from booking flights means for your travel plans
articles.summary:
Wouldn't it be nice to tell an AI assistant to find the cheapest flight to your destination and book your favorite seat while you do something else? That kind of convenience is getting closer. But United Airlines wants to make sure an unauthorized AI assistant never gets that far.

The airline is restricting third-party AI agents from accessing its booking systems without permission. United says these tools could expose sensitive customer information and make purchases travelers never intended to authorize. The concern also extends to MileagePlus accounts, where an automated mistake could put valuable airline miles at risk.

The decision comes as AI assistants become increasingly capable of taking action on our behalf. While that sounds convenient, United is raising questions about how much control we should give software over our travel plans. Here's where United draws the line and what you need to know before letting AI handle your next flight booking.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

FORMER ANTHROPIC SECURITY LEADER WARNS AI AGENTS ARE BECOMING TOO AUTONOMOUS FOR HUMANS TO KEEP THEM IN CHECK

On Nov. 11, United Airlines published an official news release titled United Restricts Access for Third-Party AI Agents. The airline explained that protecting customer information and account security prompted the restrictions. According to United, sharing account credentials with personal AI assistants can expose sensitive information. The airline also warned that automated actions might lead to unwanted purchases or changes to existing reservations. Then there's the issue of frequent flyer miles. United specifically mentioned the possibility that an AI assistant could use MileagePlus miles without the traveler intending that redemption.

To address those concerns, United is restricting unauthorized personal AI agents from accessing its digital platforms. The rules also reach travel agencies and booking services that might use automated AI tools to access United's systems. United says it is updating its policies to support these restrictions. The airline also plans to continue evaluating how personal AI assistants interact with its services.

You may already use AI to research vacation destinations or figure out which airport is closest to your hotel. An AI travel agent takes that technology further by performing tasks for you. For example, you could ask an AI assistant to find a flight under $400 that arrives before dinner. Instead of simply recommending flights, an AI agent might search booking systems and attempt to complete the reservation. Some agents can also interact with websites using a browser. That means they may be able to enter personal information and complete steps that normally require you to click through a booking process.

The convenience is easy to understand. However, granting an AI assistant access to your airline account can also give it the ability to make changes you never intended. For more on what these assistants can do, see our article on eight seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.

United's concerns go beyond account security. The airline also warns that automated AI activity could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations. Consider what happens when you check in for a flight. Airlines require travelers to acknowledge important safety information, including whether their bags contain prohibited hazardous materials.

United specifically points to the requirement for a person to confirm that baggage contains no banned substances, such as explosives. An AI assistant handling check-in could potentially bypass that acknowledgment. After all, how would an AI assistant know what you actually packed in your suitcase? United has identified this as a potential regulatory concern. The airline has not established that every AI-assisted check-in violates federal law.

This may be the biggest concern for travelers experimenting with automated booking tools. United revised its Contract of Carriage on Nov. 11. The updated rules prohibit AI agents from making or modifying tickets and purchasing airline products or services.

The contract also identifies reservations made or changed through AI agents as subject to cancellation without advance notice. The definition of an AI agent includes automated tools even when a traveler supervises or approves their actions. However, there is an important exception for existing reservations.

United says bookings made by AI agents before Nov. 11, will not be canceled under the new restriction. The airline recommends reviewing those reservations to confirm that they were properly booked and ticketed. If you previously used an AI assistant to arrange United travel, open the United app or website and verify your itinerary. Check that your ticket was actually issued rather than assuming a booking confirmation means everything is complete. You can review the airline's published rules in its Contract of Carriage at united.com/en/us/fly/contract-of-carriage.html.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

Yes, although United has established limits on how outside AI tools can interact with its systems. You can still ask an AI chatbot for general travel advice or help creating an itinerary. United's guidance allows AI-assisted research and trip planning as long as the tool does not access United's website or app. However, an unauthorized AI agent cannot search United's website or app on your behalf. The restriction also covers automated purchasing and reservation management. That means an AI-powered browser feature that automatically searches United's website could fall under the restriction, even if it never buys a ticket.

United says assistive technology for travelers with disabilities remains unaffected. Traditional travel booking services can also continue operating through permitted channels. The restriction specifically addresses unauthorized AI agents, including those used by travel agencies. According to United's published guidance, the airline does not currently work with any third-party AI agents under this policy.

While United is putting restrictions in place, Southwest Airlines is exploring a different approach. On Oct. 6, Southwest announced a ChatGPT integration. The feature allows you to discover destinations and shop for Southwest flights directly through ChatGPT. However, Southwest's integration still directs you to the airline's website to complete purchases. The company describes the arrangement as an early step toward broader AI-powered booking capabilities.

That approach gives Southwest a way to use AI for flight discovery while maintaining control over the final transaction. United is taking a more restrictive position on outside AI assistants. The airline says it will continue evaluating the technology as it develops.

If you normally book flights through United's website or app, you can continue doing so. You can also use permitted travel booking services. However, if you've started experimenting with AI assistants that make purchases or manage accounts on your behalf, United's restrictions deserve your attention. An AI agent with access to your airline account could potentially reach sensitive travel information. Depending on its permissions, it might also make purchases you never intended to authorize. Here are a few ways to protect yourself.

Avoid giving third-party AI assistants your MileagePlus password or other sensitive login information. If you've already shared your credentials with an AI agent, United recommends changing your password immediately. You should also remove any saved login details from the AI service. Consider using a password manager to create and securely store a strong, unique password for your airline account. This can help protect your account if a password you use elsewhere gets exposed in a data breach.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your devices from malware and malicious links designed to steal login credentials. This is especially important if you use travel booking websites or receive airline confirmation emails. While antivirus protection won't stop an AI assistant from making an unauthorized reservation, it can help prevent cybercriminals from gaining access to your MileagePlus account. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Use United's official website or app, or a booking provider operating under United's rules. United currently does not work with third-party AI agents under this policy. Even if an AI assistant offers to complete a reservation with your approval, that does not necessarily make the transaction permissible.

UNITED AIRLINES SAYS TECHNOLOGY ISSUE RESOLVED AFTER ‘WIDESPREAD SYSTEM OUTAGE’

Review your MileagePlus balance for unexpected activity. If you notice a redemption or purchase you don't recognize, secure your account immediately. Contact United through its official website or app to report the activity and request assistance.

Check your booking confirmation and make sure United has issued your ticket. If an AI assistant arranged your travel before Nov. 11, verify the reservation directly with the airline. United says those earlier bookings will not be canceled under the new restriction.

AI can still help you plan a trip using general information without accessing United's systems. However, complete your flight purchases and reservation changes yourself through permitted channels. That way, you can review what you're buying without risking a prohibited AI-agent transaction.

I can see why United is concerned. I've spent enough time searching for flights to appreciate the idea of handing that job over to AI. Let the assistant find me a great fare and save me the hassle of comparing a dozen options. I'm all for that. But the moment it starts making purchases or accessing my airline miles, I want to know exactly what it's doing.

I recently spoke with travel expert Katy Nastro, who discovered that someone had stolen 50,000 miles from her American Airlines account. Her experience had nothing to do with AI agents, but it reminded me how much value we keep in these loyalty programs. I certainly wouldn't want an automated mistake putting those rewards at risk.

At the same time, I do wonder whether security is the only concern driving United's decision. Airlines have spent years building direct relationships with travelers. AI agents could change how we compare fares and choose which airline gets our business. I would hate to see useful technology held back simply because it gives you more control over the shopping process. United says it will keep evaluating these tools, and I hope that eventually leads to a secure way to book flights using AI. Until then, I'm happy to let AI help find my next trip. I'll take care of the booking myself.

Would you trust an AI assistant to book your next flight and access your frequent flyer miles? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter

articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
articles.summary:
Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.

Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.

The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.

Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.

Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.

Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.

For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.

When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.

The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
articles.summary:
Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected?

That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended.

Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps.

Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step.

Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working.

Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing.

One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose.

For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods.

Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions.

Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf.

MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR

Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported.

These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions.

There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward.

That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate.

You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available.

Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS.

If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs.

Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure.

When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access.

If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information.

Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes.

Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy.

An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use.

If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer.

I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update.

Would you trust an AI assistant with unrestricted access to your Mac if it could save you hours of work, or does the thought of software reading your private information cross a line? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Ex- Ukraine prosecutor general accuses Zelenskyy's office of interfering in anti-corruption investigation
articles.summary:
Ukraine's former prosecutor general is accusing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's administration of interfering in a criminal investigation involving the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau after the president demanded his removal from office in September.

In an extensive interview with Fox News Digital, Ruslan Kravchenko alleged that Zelenskyy's decision to remove him came under pressure from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), whose officials he said his office had been investigating.

"The signature on the resignation letter was mine. The decision was his," Kravchenko said. "You do not have to put handcuffs on the president himself to tie his hands. It is enough to put the people he relies on at risk."

BILLIONS IN US AID TO UKRAINE UNDER MICROSCOPE AS CORRUPTION ROCKS ZELENSKYY’S INNER CIRCLE

Kravchenko's most serious allegation concerns what happened afterward. He claims the president's office instructed prosecutors to close a criminal case involving NABU Director Semen Kryvonos.

"The Office of the President began issuing instructions to the Office of the Prosecutor General to immediately close the criminal case against the head of NABU," he said. "In my assessment, that amounts to deliberate interference in an investigation."

"The authority to investigate crimes becomes the ability to determine government policy and even geopolitics," he argued.

Kravchenko did not identify who allegedly issued those instructions or provide documentary evidence of the communications in the materials supplied to Fox News Digital. His allegation of presidential interference has not been independently verified.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Kravchenko's departure followed a September investigation known as Operation Carthage, in which NABU and SAPO accused officials connected to the Prosecutor General's Office of helping protect fraudulent call centers and laundering criminal proceeds.

According to a Sept. 8 report in The Guardian, the investigation centered on fraudulent call centers whose employees impersonated banks, police officers and investment advisers to steal money from victims in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. NABU alleged that a senior official in the Prosecutor General's Office protected the operation and helped launder its proceeds. 

Law enforcement sources told Ukrainska Pravda that individual call centers paid approximately $7,000 a month in protection money. Investigators also released recordings suggesting that the principal suspect had overseen repairs at Kravchenko's home while allegedly collecting bribes.

Kravchenko, who has not been charged in the investigation, denies wrongdoing and rejects the allegations against his office. He claimed the operation was intended to seize investigative materials concerning misconduct by anti-corruption officials and prevent him from pursuing those cases.

He said he initially refused to resign but changed his position following a Sept. 7 meeting with Zelenskyy, attended, according to Kravchenko, by Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the president's parliamentary faction.

"When the president wants your resignation and the leader of his parliamentary faction, which commands a majority, is sitting beside him, believe me: a prosecutor general's room for maneuver is extremely limited," he said.

Zelenskyy publicly confirmed that he had demanded Kravchenko's removal.

"There is only one path for this Prosecutor General: removal from office. That is what I told him," Zelenskyy said in a Sept. 14 statement, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy also said that if Kravchenko considered the decision political pressure, he was free to characterize it that way. The president suspended him on Sept. 14, and parliament approved his dismissal the following day.

ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

The confrontation intensified when Kravchenko announced on Sept. 14 that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos over alleged misconduct predating his appointment as NABU director.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office disputed the validity of the notice, stating that Kryvonos had not been formally notified of suspicion under Ukrainian law and that relevant entries in the investigative register had been deleted.

Kravchenko alleges those actions followed pressure from the president's administration. The claim remains unverified.

NABU and SAPO have rejected Kravchenko's broader accusations, describing them as a campaign against independent anti-corruption institutions. In a Nov. 4 announcement, the agencies said Operation Carthage had uncovered an alleged criminal network involving senior law-enforcement officials accused of protecting fraudulent businesses. Those allegations have not been proven in court.

The controversy comes amid widespread public concern about corruption. A September survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 72% of Ukrainians held Zelenskyy politically responsible for corruption among his associates, although the findings did not suggest respondents believed he was personally involved.

Zelenskyy has publicly condemned the widening investigation's allegations. In a Nov. 7 address, he described alleged misconduct involving senior security officials as "frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable," according to Reuters, and called for a full investigation.

His former chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, defended him in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, amid an earlier corruption scandal in November 2025, describing Zelenskyy as "not corrupt" and saying he had allowed independent anti-corruption investigations.

Zelenskyy's office did not respond to multiple requests from Fox News Digital for comment on Kravchenko's latest allegations.

The former prosecutor general maintains that his removal prevented him from pursuing investigations into the leadership of the anti-corruption agencies. Ukrainian authorities, meanwhile, have publicly defended the investigation that preceded his dismissal.

articles.title: Former Florida mayor urges American Jews to fight back against rising antisemitism
articles.summary:
As antisemitism surges across the United States and around the world in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, policy strategist and public speaker Gabe Groisman is urging American Jews to stand their ground and fight for the future of their community — and the soul of the nation.

In his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America," Groisman, a former mayor of Bal Harbour, Florida, explores the history of American Jews and their contributions to the country, arguing that despite rising antisemitism, they should confront the tide of hate and stand firm in their rightful place.

"The first fight we have to take on here in the U.S. is to strengthen the community, to try to teach our brothers and sisters about who we are as a people," Groisman told Fox News Digital. "Then we can get to the part of why the Land of Israel is important to us, why Jewish sovereignty over the Land of Israel, which is the State of Israel today, is an integral part of who we are as Jews in America or anywhere in the world."

CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND

One of the book’s chapters opens with quotes from Genesis. Groisman explained that powerful forces are seeking to distance American Jews from Israel. On the left, he said, a movement is seeking to "unlearn Zionism," while on the right, critics attack Zionism through the lens of dual loyalty.

"These days, people are afraid to connect things to the Bible, but it is critical to do so. It is the only way to honestly understand where our connection to that land begins. It begins with the Bible and the words of God himself," Groisman said.

He noted that only 26% of American Jews say they believe in "God as described in the Bible," per a Pew Research Center study published in May 2021. According to the study, another 50% believe in some other spiritual force.

"Most American Jews don't hold a biblical or Judeo-Christian understanding of God, and I think that's a huge reason why most don't look to the Bible for their connection to the land," said Groisman.

"When they are asked to defend their connection to the Land of Israel or to the State of Israel, they can’t begin to respond in a proper way because they don’t believe in God," he added.

Groisman has practiced law for more than 20 years, litigating cases nationwide and participating in legal challenges on behalf of the Jewish community.

A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT

During his tenure as mayor, Groisman passed what he describes as the nation's first anti-Israel boycott ordinance, as well as the first municipal ordinance adopting a definition of antisemitism.

Groisman said the book seeks to address a question American Jews across the country are asking privately: What is the future of Jews in America, and is it time to leave? His answer, he said, is an emphatic no.

"Jewish American history is not well taught, not even in Jewish circles. We need to understand that this community has been here since before day one and has played integral roles in this country. The religious liberties established in this country from the beginning were meant to benefit groups explicitly like the Jews, who were here from day one," he said.

For American Jews, Groisman said, the solution lies in helping young people reconnect with their identity. He argued that a strong sense of identity and purpose, rooted in their Jewish religion and national heritage, can help them become confident American Jews and thrive in the United States.

"America is not about freedom from religion; it’s about freedom of religion. You are allowed to be who you are as an American and still be as American as everybody else," he said.

In his book, Groisman examines developments over the past several years that he believes have contributed to the surge in antisemitism, including the rise of intersectionality and critical race theory on the left and their growing influence in academic and intellectual circles, which he says have received significant funding from foreign actors.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Groisman pointed to foreign funding flowing into American universities, warning that "that money comes with strings attached" and is intended "to create chaos in our country." He argued that foreign actors unable to defeat the United States militarily seek to weaken it by creating internal divisions, with antisemitism serving as "a useful tool" in that effort.

"When we saw actors in this country, in the aftermath of Oct. 7 and even before Israel responded in Gaza, being coordinated and directed by foreign actors in the United States, all the way down to small chapters on college campuses across the country, that requires years and years of coordination," he said.

Groisman said his book offers a message of optimism, emphasizing his faith in America, its political system and the American people’s ability to confront these challenges.

"For the American Jewish community, this book will hopefully help swing the pendulum back, encouraging people to recalibrate and put our country — and the American Jewish community as an integral part of it — back on track," he said.

articles.title: Iran flogs female singer 74 times for performing without hijab in viral YouTube concert
articles.summary:
Iranian authorities subjected a female singer and four members of her concert team to 74 lashes each Monday after she defied the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on women by performing without a hijab in a viral YouTube concert, their lawyers said.

Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and her four male co-defendants were flogged in the Iranian city of Qom, defense attorney Mostafa Nili told Iranian news outlet Emtedad, according to Reuters.

The five were also banned from traveling abroad and engaging in artistic and musical activities for two years.

IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN

One of the defendants’ lawyers told the BBC Monday that efforts to overturn the ruling, reduce the punishment or suspend its enforcement had failed. Defense attorneys also sought to postpone the flogging, but authorities insisted on carrying out the sentence immediately.

The punishment sparked outrage among Iranian artists and human rights advocates, who condemned the regime’s restrictions on women and artistic expression.

Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), told the BBC that Ahmadi’s flogging was "a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights" and demonstrated the authorities’ determination to suppress women’s freedoms and punish those who challenge discriminatory laws.

Those flogged alongside Ahmadi were musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia and producer Mohsen Lashkari.

IRAN REGIME'S EXECUTION SPREE CONTINUES AS TWINS FACE DEATH PENALTY, DECADES IN PRISON AFTER ALLEGED TORTURE

The case stems from a Dec. 11, 2024, performance in which Ahmadi appeared in a sleeveless black dress with her hair uncovered, accompanied by male musicians at the historic Deir Gachin Caravanserai in Qom province.

With no audience physically present, Ahmadi shared the performance, known as the "Imaginary Concert," on her YouTube channel.

The video of the concert has garnered over 3 million views on YouTube.

Iran’s judiciary swiftly opened a criminal case over the performance, and Ahmadi was arrested three days later. Two musicians involved in the concert were also arrested. All three were subsequently released on bail, according to the Norway-based Hengaw Organization for Human Rights.

In June 2026, a criminal court in Qom sentenced Ahmadi and eight others involved in the production to 74 lashes each on charges of "offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online," according to Hengaw.

The defendants denied the charges. An appeals court upheld the flogging sentences in September, clearing the way for their enforcement, Iran International reported Sept. 25.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Amnesty International urged Iranian authorities in October to abandon plans to carry out the sentences, arguing that judicial flogging amounts to torture and violates international human rights protections.

Ahmadi, a native of Nowshahr in northern Iran who studied film directing at Soore University, had previously faced restrictions from Iranian security authorities over her performances of protest songs and regional folk music during the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, according to Hengaw.

The movement erupted in September 2022 following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman detained by the country’s morality police for allegedly violating mandatory hijab rules.

Many Iranian women have since openly defied the compulsory dress code, despite periodic arrests, warnings and other enforcement measures.

Of the nine people originally sentenced over Ahmadi’s concert, five were reported to have been flogged Monday. The status of the remaining defendants’ punishments remains unclear.

Ahmadi’s punishment comes amid a broader human rights crackdown in Iran that has intensified since nationwide anti-regime protests erupted in January. In addition to years of restrictions on women, artists, journalists and political dissidents, Iranian authorities have increasingly resorted to mass arrests, torture in detention and executions to suppress opposition, as previously reported by Fox News Digital.
