articles.summary: Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday claimed attacks targeting the financial district in the Saudi capital and the sprawling Ras Tanura refinery in the kingdom's oil-rich east, in retaliation for strikes on their territory. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree described the attack targeting the refinery as "accurate and direct", saying it "caused fires to break out at the facility". He said the attack on Riyadh was "carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately".

articles.title: Cyberattack exposes unclassified information from CIA system, US media reports
articles.summary: A recently discovered hack on a CIA analysis system exposed some unclassified information, US media reported on Tuesday. The breach is the latest in a series of cyber attacks that have targeted US government departments and major companies in recent weeks.

articles.title: 🔴 Surprise Eurostar strike cancels London, Paris and Brussels trains
🔴 Colombia president says all hostages freed, one assailant killed after supermarket hostage siege
AFCON 2025: CAS gives title back to Senegal as Morocco vows to challenge verdict
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has handed down its ruling: Senegal is officially the 2025 AFCON champion. The Moroccan Football Federation has announced that it will challenge the verdict, citing irregularities in the proceedings.

articles.title: Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
articles.summary: Amnesty International on Wednesday urged the International Criminal Court to investigate whether Israeli officials committed genocide in Gaza, citing measures it says have prevented births and severely harmed women's reproductive health. The rights group said it had serious concerns that these effects were intentional, while acknowledging it could not reach a definitive conclusion.

articles.title: Live: Two Libyan soldiers killed in Ukrainian attack on Russian vessels in Benghazi
articles.summary: Two Libyan soldiers have died from injuries sustained in an attack, claimed by Ukraine, on Russian ships near Benghazi, a senior figure in the administration in eastern Libya said late on Tuesday. Members of the European Parliament will convene in Strasbourg on Wednesday to discuss "Europe’s role and capacity to protect the international order and secure a just and lasting peace for Ukraine". Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks €115 billion in foreign aid for 2027, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Ukraine will need €115 billion in external financing next year to sustain its economy and war effort against Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, adding that Kyiv had secured commitments for about €90 billion from the European Union.

articles.title: New York jury convicts Huawei of stealing trade secrets
articles.summary: A New York jury on Tuesday found Chinese telecom giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and other criminal offences, but acquitted it of a racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. The verdict followed a three-month trial in New York in a case that adds to longstanding US efforts to curb Huawei's operations over alleged threats to national security.

articles.title: Champions League: Real Madrid thrash PSV 5-1 in comeback win as Manchester City held by Napoli
articles.summary: Real Madrid extended their winning run to 10 games in all competitions on Tuesday, overturning an early deficit to rout PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in the Champions League, with Jude Bellingham scoring a spectacular goal and Kylian Mbappé netting twice. Manchester City, meanwhile, twice came from behind to draw 2-2 with Napoli, while Arsenal were held to a 1-1 draw by Borussia Dortmund.

articles.title: Tech executives' investment in Trump 'clearly paying off' as Huang reinstated at Nvidia
articles.summary: Nvidia shares fell on Tuesday as the historic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return as CEO quickly lost steam, with investors refocusing ​on the political ‌and governance risks surrounding his reinstatement. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, The Hill Senior Technology Reporter Miranda Nazzaro says that the reinstatement of Huang at Nvidia represents "the culmination of a two-year push of tech executives to get closer to President Trump and their investment in the president is clearly paying off".

articles.title: Tech executives' investment in Trump 'clearly paying off' as Huang reinstated at Nvidia
articles.summary: Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, The Hill Senior Technology Reporter Miranda Nazzaro says that the reinstatement of Jensen Huang at Nvidia represents "the culmination of a two-year push of tech executives to get closer to President Trump and their investment in the president is clearly paying off".

articles.title: 'Quid pro quo’: Nvidia too big to fail or ‘too close to personal interest of people around Trump’?
articles.summary: Angela Diffley is pleased to welcome Bernard Benhamou, Secretary General of the Institute of Digital Sovereignty and Senior Lecturer in Internet Governance at Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University. What does Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia mean for Trump, Lutnick, the US, the AI industry and China? Describing Huang as “the global banker of the AI industry”, Benhamou explains: “He is the visionary, he is the banker. He's not only the chip maker.” He also warns of the repercussions of Donald Trump's decision to reinstate the Nvidia CEO, with congressional and judicial scrutiny looming. “It's far from over. It's just the beginning.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia comeback sends AI videos into overdrive
articles.summary: Just 11 days after resigning as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang's return has unleashed a fresh wave of AI-generated videos. But the internet has changed its tune: while last week's memes mocked Huang, many now celebrate his comeback. One viral video purportedly showing him dancing is actually AI-manipulated footage of a basketball coach from 2016. From humiliation to hero worship, the technology Nvidia helped popularise is rewriting the narrative surrounding its own CEO, as Vedika Bahl explains.

articles.title: Did Nvidia knowingly send chips to China 'cutout'? Was there 'pay-to-play' involving Trump, Lutnick?
articles.summary: François Picard is pleased to welcome Andrew Weissmann, Professor of Practice at NYU School of Law and a former federal prosecutor known for leading major Department of Justice (DOJ) and FBI investigations. Professor Weissmann joins us to discuss the legal and ethical questions surrounding the Trump administration's dealings with chipmaker Nvidia following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as president and CEO.

articles.title: Senegal reinstated as AFCON 2025 winners
articles.summary: In tonight's edition: Senegal are reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winners after sport's highest court upheld their appeal against being stripped of the title. We bring you reactions and analysis from our Sports Journalist James Vasina.

articles.title: UN slams Iran after it flogs singer for performing without veil
articles.summary: The United Nations condemned as "abhorrent" the flogging of Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her production team, urging Tehran to abolish the practice. The five received 74 lashes each on Monday following a performance viewed millions of times on YouTube, local media reported, citing Ahmadi's lawyer.

articles.title: Russian nuclear satellites plan 'foolhardy', expert says
articles.summary: NATO chief Mark Rutte said Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Jennie Shin, Dafydd Townley, Senior Teaching Fellow in International Security at the University of Portsmouth, says that the alleged plan would be "foolhardy because the impact would be indiscriminate, they wouldn't be able to choose only Western or non-Russian satellites".

articles.title: The Bukele method: Will Salvadoran leader's strong-arm tactics work for Haiti?
articles.summary: Haitians are hailing the Bukele method. Citizens of the Americas' poorest nation are cheering the Salvadoran president’s "shoot first, ask questions later" method of dealing with the gangs that have overrun their country for the past six years. Can the police force deployed actually restore law and order? We ask about the latest in a decades-long list of efforts by the international community to support Haiti.

articles.title: Senegal AFCON ruling 'good in the books of sports law', expert says
articles.summary: Speaking with FRANCE 24's Jennie Shin, sports presenter and journalist Thando Sibiya explains that the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport to reinstate Senegal as ⁠winner of ​the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations "from a jurisprudence perspective or creating precedent, it is going to be good in the books of sports law, because if every single decision of a referee is taken to a court of law all the time, it really tampers with the quality, governance and legitimacy of the game".

articles.title: Senegal regain AFCON title on appeal at Morocco's expense
articles.summary: Senegal on Tuesday regained their Africa Cup of Nations title after winning an appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) against the decision by the Confederation of African Football to declare Morocco the winners following a chaotic final in January. CAS said in a statement it had "upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF)" by a "unanimous decision". FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports.

articles.title: 'Nothing will ever be the same' for Jensen Huang and Nvidia after his return
articles.summary: PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, November 24: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia dominates the papers. In other news, leaked records shed new light on Russian military losses in Ukraine. Also, the UK will host the 2035 Women's World Cup. Finally, a devilled eggs world championship crowns its winner.

articles.title: Nvidia's position as cornerstone of AI trade confirmed by market reaction to Huang's return
articles.summary: Tech shares in Asia and Europe rebounded on Tuesday, following in the footsteps of Nvidia's shares closing on Wall Street 31 percent higher on Monday. The return of CEO Jensen Huang, 11 days after his resignation over an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has reassured investors in the AI trade. In this edition, we look at Nvidia's central role in this trade, and Huang's central role at Nvidia. Also, French President Emmanuel Macron proposes to enshrine fiscal rules in the constitution.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: In a stunning U-turn, Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as the company's president and CEO. The announcement came just days after the board rejected a petition calling for the tech titan's return. US President Donald Trump said had personally got in touch with the board to advocate for Huang's return. Nvidia's stock surged 32 percent on the news, adding nearly $1 trillion to its market cap while the rest of Wall Street also rallied.

articles.title: 'It can take years': Why the AI Riemann proof is far from settled
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence claimed another major scalp in maths on Friday, as Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge published what he says is proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a Millennium Prize Problem, in 17 million lines of code that no human has read in full. Physicist Tony Padilla tells Tech 24 that verification could take years, and that Alpöge should share how he got there.

articles.title: 'GTA VI': When the biggest-ever entertainment release becomes the biggest headline
articles.summary: This week FRANCE 24's media show "Scoop" looks at how the press covered the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI". Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than $2.3 billion. What does the game and the franchise's success mean for the future of entertainment? Our guest is Margaret Wallace, a video game developer and an associate professor of the practice of media innovation at Boston University.

articles.title: Anthropic shares slide on second day of trading as AI jitters fuel tech sell-off
articles.summary: Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as ​nosediving tech stocks showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. Shares in the AI firm dipped below $90, one day after soaring to over $110 during a record-breaking Nasdaq debut.

articles.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
articles.summary: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34 percent higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17 percent. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.

articles.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
articles.summary: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?

articles.title: Anthropic blows past $2 trillion in Nasdaq debut, beating SpaceX's June listing
articles.summary: Anthropic hit $2 trillion in market value as its shares soared in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, with investors rushing to own a stake in the maker of the Claude chatbot, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company. Shares began trading at $111.5, 34% higher than the IPO price of $83.

articles.title: AI lab Anthropic sets stock market record with $81 billion IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic becomes the first "pure play" AI lab to go public, with an eye-watering $1.5 trillion valuation, a bellwether moment amid growing concerns of a financial bubble in the sector. Meanwhile, a scientific study shows US data centres are emitting as much greenhouse gas as entire nations.

articles.title: Inside Limoges city hall, devastated by arson attack during French riots
articles.summary: Work is underway to restore the city hall of Limoges, in central France, which was devastated by an arson attack during riots on October 17. More than €1.7 million has been raised through an online fundraising campaign in the wake of the disaster. Also on the show, the highly anticipated video game "Grand Theft Auto VI" has finally been released, with gamers in Oceania among the first to get a taste of the latest instalment in the franchise.

articles.title: 'Extreme wealth can become a type of brain damage': Journalist Alexander Hurst
articles.summary: An international journalist who poured his meagre savings into highly risky options trading at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic and quickly made $1.2 million, before losing it all again, has spoken to FRANCE 24 about his experience. Alexander Hurst works for a number of media outlets, including the Guardian as a correspondent based in Paris.

articles.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
articles.summary: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.

articles.title: Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote
articles.summary: Ahead of local elections, AI-generated falsehoods targeting Democratic Progressive Party mayoral candidate Puma Shen have surged in Taiwan, alongside disinformation claiming the US is pulling back support for the island.

articles.title: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.

articles.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
articles.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.

articles.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

articles.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
articles.summary: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

articles.title: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
articles.summary: Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.

articles.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
articles.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation continues. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.

articles.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
articles.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.

articles.title: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
articles.summary: Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

articles.title: After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
articles.summary: Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled at Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at the APEC summit.

articles.title: Nepal's new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
articles.summary: On his first foreign bilateral visit, rapper-turned-Prime Minister Balendra Shah sought deeper ties with Nepal's neighbor and largest trading partner, while steering clear of sticky territorial issues.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates former CEO Jensen Huang despite China espionage scandal
articles.summary: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring back the disgraced CEO, who resigned this month amid news of his affairs. He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset.

articles.title: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate
articles.summary: EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute involving Bulgaria.

articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

articles.title: COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy
articles.summary: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

articles.title: 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
articles.summary: For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

articles.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
articles.summary: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

articles.title: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading
articles.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

articles.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
articles.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

articles.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
articles.summary: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

articles.title: Parliament clears 7 EU budget files for negotiations
articles.summary:
The European Parliament voted by large majorities to send seven proposals for the EU’s next long-term budget straight into negotiations with the Council, heading off a possible challenge from the far right.

The lawmakers were voting on the proposals for Global Europe, the European Social Fund, Horizon Europe, the Connecting Europe Facility, the European Competitiveness Fund, the asylum and migration program and AgoraEU. 

These proposals are now moving to negotiations with the Council of the European Union based on reports adopted by the committees responsible for each file.

articles.title: Sánchez to skip EU summit before Spanish election
articles.summary:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will delegate his voting powers to French President Emmanuel Macron as he won’t be able to attend the European Council summit on Thursday and Friday, according to an EU diplomat. 

Spain heads to the polls on Sunday, with Sánchez at risk of losing his parliamentary majority. On Thursday evening, he will face conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, far-right leader Santiago Abascal and left-wing alliance chief Ada Colau in the final debate of the campaign.

Wielding Spain’s vote as well as his own, Macron will have extra leverage at a summit dominated by bilateral negotiations between leaders.

The extraordinary summit will kick off Thursday with a discussion among all leaders on the EU budget and a €45 billion loan to Ukraine, followed by several hours of restricted meetings, two EU diplomats said. Leaders will reconvene Friday morning to advance negotiations.

Leaders will also sign off on the appointment of Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next European Central Bank chief on Friday morning, with Macron casting Spain’s vote as well.

Sánchez has opted for a liberal leader from another big country, rather than delegating to fellow center-left figures such as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen or Malta’s Robert Abela.

Sánchez and Frederiksen have clashed over migration policy since the Danish leader teamed up with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to demand tougher border controls following the crisis in Spain’s enclave of Ceuta on the Moroccan border.

Europe’s Social Democrats are set to formally discuss Frederiksen’s hard line on migration, particularly her backing for deportation hubs in Rwanda.

This article was updated.

articles.title: He’s coming home: Catalan leader Puigdemont plans return to Spain
articles.summary:
Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont will return to Barcelona on Dec. 12, ending nearly a decade of self-imposed exile in Belgium.

“I will return to Catalonia without asking for permission and without asking for forgiveness,” Puigdemont said at a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday. The former Catalan president initially fled to Belgium in October 2017 to avoid prosecution over his role in the region’s 2017 unauthorized independence referendum.

Spanish authorities spent years trying to extradite the separatist leader but Belgian judges repeatedly thwarted their efforts. In 2024, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opened the door to his return by securing the passage of a sweeping amnesty for those involved in the independence movement in exchange for crucial support from Puigdemont’s center-right Junts party.

Spanish courts refused to apply the amnesty to Puigdemont, but after the EU’s top court ruled that he should benefit from the measure, Spain’s Constitutional Court this week lifted the remaining charges.

In a 2024 interview with POLITICO, Puigdemont said he yearned to return to his hometown of Girona and “become anonymous once again.”

On Wednesday, however, he hinted at a renewed leading role in the separatist movement. “We need to update the strategy because we have learned from our mistakes,” he said, adding that he remained “committed to the independence of Catalonia.”

His return could set the stage for a fresh confrontation with Madrid if the center-right People’s Party and far-right Vox emerge as the winners from Sunday’s snap election. Among other measures, both parties want to dissolve political forces that promote independence.

articles.title: Von der Leyen: Energy ceasefire would show Putin is serious about peace talks
articles.summary:
STRASBOURG — Vladimir Putin’s agreement to a winter energy ceasefire and a Black Sea truce to allow Ukrainian food exports “would show that Russia is serious about negotiations,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday morning.

“As discussed at last week’s coalition of the willing meeting, Russia should agree to a winter ceasefire on energy infrastructure, and a truce to ensure the safe passage of food exports through the Black Sea,” she told European lawmakers at a Parliament debate in Strasbourg. Von der Leyen met with the coalition to discuss the European position on Ukraine-Russia peace talks brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump.

She added the Commission was helping strengthen Kyiv’s hand at the negotiations by stepping up sanctions and providing cash so as to put pressure on Russia, which persistently bombards cities across Ukraine in an unrelenting military assault.

The Commission on Monday proposed its 22nd sanctions package, which includes transaction bans on more Russian banks, restrictions on European companies helping Russia develop or maintain its energy infrastructure, an EU visa ban on current and former members of Russia’s armed forces, and a ban on Europeans sitting on the governing bodies of Russian companies.

Sanctions “erode the foundations of Russia’s war, and we have many indicators pointing to a worsening outlook of the Russian economy,” she said.

The strategy is twofold, she said: “First, maximum support for Ukraine, combined with maximum pressure on Russia. And second, full European engagement in negotiations for lasting peace.”

She added that Europe’s financial support was a key part of the peace talks, and outlined the new loan structure to cover Ukraine’s 2027 needs, including €45 billion provided by the EU.

“A strong European team will participate in the next round of talks,” she vowed. “We will judge progress based on Russia’s actions, not simply on its words.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s raid in Libya damaged more than a Russian warship
articles.summary:
Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.

Ukraine’s attack on a Russian warship in a Libyan port was a striking military success. It may also have broken international law.

“An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war” was how Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded Sunday’s sinking of the Merkury, one of Russia’s most advanced corvettes, docked at the time in Benghazi. Ukraine’s leader proudly announced on his Telegram channel that the operation, involving seven Ukrainian-made sea drones, had also disabled a Russian cargo ship suspected of transporting weapons.

From a military perspective the operation was indeed another one of Ukraine’s audacious commando missions. It was reminiscent of the derring-do spirit of Winston Churchill’s “Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare,” better known as the Special Operations Executive, which mounted commando raids along the French coast, causing havoc and raising British wartime morale during WWII .

In fact, the day before, while visiting Kyiv, Britain’s defense secretary Wes Streeting had coincidentally compared Zelenskyy to Britain’s iconic wartime leader.

The comparison was ironic given the circumstances. Despite Churchill’s impatience and determination to take the fight to the enemy, the wartime prime minister was careful to avoid breaching the laws of armed conflict at sea. He didn’t, for example, order British warships to sink the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee when it was cornered in Montevideo after the Battle of the River Plate. The trapped warship’s captain ultimately decided to scuttle the ship.

But Zelenskyy wasn’t so restrained this week. According to international legal scholars, the attack likely violated international law as well as Libya’s sovereignty. The country’s eastern administration, based in Benghazi, has called on the U.N. to investigate the sinking as well as “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts or military units” in western Libya.

The Libyans would have a good case if they lodged a complaint with the International Court of Justice, said David Letts, a retired Australian naval officer and now director of the military law program at the Australian National University in Canberra. “Unless you’re wanting to mount an argument that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and neutrality doesn’t apply, I’m struggling to see how this sinking sits within the law,” Letts said.

Letts is one of the authors of the Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare, a compilation of legislation published and updated by the U.S. Naval War College. He says Ukraine’s Benghazi attack is “quite different when compared to their strikes against Russian vessels in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports” in disputed and not neutral waters.

The laws of neutrality are largely based on the 1907 Hague Convention, which codified the rights and duties of non-belligerent states during armed conflicts. Under it, countries at war are prohibited from conducting attacks, blockades or mine-laying within neutral waters. In return, neutral states shouldn’t let belligerent warships turn their ports into military bases. Stays are generally limited to 24 hours, with exceptions for damage, repairs or poor weather.

“The attack was a violation of Libya’s neutrality,” said James Kraska of the U.S. Naval War College and professor of international maritime law in the Stockton Center for International Law. “An attack is lawful if it’s beyond 12 nautical miles from the coastline, but, of course, inside it’s a violation.”

“Now on the Ukrainian side, what their argument might be is that a belligerent warship ought only to stay 24 hours in a foreign neutral port. If it goes beyond 24 hours, then the warship is at risk, and Libya might not be in compliance,” Kraska, a retired U.S. Navy commander, told POLITICO. “If there’s inclement weather, or repairs are needed to make it seaworthy, then the time can be extended,” he added. Some scholars, he added, would argue that Ukraine would need to contact the Libyan authorities to find out the status.

In terms of its boldness and reach, Monday’s attack wasn’t entirely unprecedented. In March, Libyan authorities reported damage to the Russian gas tanker Arctic Metagaz while it was en route to Egypt. Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the tanker with naval drones likely launched from Western Libya. Kyiv neither confirmed nor denied its involvement.

The governments of Sudan, Mali and Niger have also accused Ukrainian special forces of mounting operations in their countries, where Russian mercenary soldiers are present. Kyiv has denied those allegations.

This time, though, Kyiv has proudly admitted sinking the Merkury in a neutral port. Why? And does the breach of law on neutrality actually matter? Zelenskyy’s office didn’t respond to questions from POLITICO on the sinking, including as to whether it had sought counsel from senior government law officers before approving the attack, and whether it had notified Libyan authorities beforehand to request the ship leave Benghazi.

In the past, when questions of neutrality have arisen or Ukraine has been accused of breaching the laws of warfare, Kyiv has said this is no time for niceties as it is the aggrieved nation. When a U.N. monitoring mission in 2023 alleged abuse of Russian POWs, for example, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry thanked the mission for documenting Russia’s violations but pushed back on the claims against Kyiv, arguing: “We consider it unacceptable to place responsibility on the victim of aggression.”

Former U.K. diplomat Tim Willasey-Wilsey, now a fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, says that when it comes to the sinking of the Merkury, he doesn’t believe the legal issues are important. “Who gives a stuff, really, you know? To be honest, I don’t think the legality particularly matters.”

He said the biggest political risk for Kyiv is diminishing the “remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine,” and so was reassured when Wes Streeting came out so quickly in support. The attack, he said, reflected desperation in Ukraine, where ballistic missile attacks are devastating civilian infrastructure, itself a violation by Russia of international law. “The war is clearly getting more and more visceral, and I think the timing of the Benghazi attack is testimony to the sense of desperation that there is now in Kyiv.”

But turning a blind eye to the Benghazi attack only adds to the erosion of international legal norms and the undermining of the post-1945 “rules-based international order,” which Moscow and Beijing have little time for. It makes the seas more dangerous.

Letts stressed how important it is for countries like Ukraine to stick to what’s legal. “I wonder what the attitude would be if this vessel had been docked in Genoa or Southampton, say, rather than Benghazi,” he added. “I think there’s an element here of ‘It was only over there, so it doesn’t really matter.’”

“Having built up a body of law that tries to protect victims of armed conflict, tries to limit the scope of armed conflicts, are we willing to wave goodbye to all of that?” he asked. “Are we willing just to have total warfare with all the rules gone and to say, ‘The last 100 years or so are a waste of time. Do whatever you want.’ I don’t think we are.”

articles.title: EU Commission failed to deliver cage ban, court finds
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission “failed to act” on a promised ban on cages in farming and can’t ignore successful citizen initiatives, according to a court ruling Wednesday.

“The Commission has failed to follow up on its intention to put an end to the farming of certain species and categories of animals,” said the General Court, part of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

The Commission must now set a timeline for phasing out cages for calves, rabbits, ducks and other farmed animals.

Animal welfare groups can celebrate a win after bringing the case in 2024, accusing the EU executive of ignoring a European Citizens’ Initiative to ban cages for all farmed animals.

The ruling, while a win for NGOs, has its caveats. The court does not detail by when the Commission must act. What’s more, the EU executive could still avoid taking action if it formally withdraws its promise to phase out cages for these animals.

Following the initiative, which gained almost 1.4 million signatures, the former Commission promised in 2021 to deliver a timeline for banning cages for a list of animals before the end of 2023. When that did not happen, a group of NGOs sued the Commission.

The Commission is obliged to follow through on the promises it made in response to the ECI, regardless of a change in the assembly of commissioners, according to the court.

The NGO leading the case, Compassion in World Farming, said the Commission confirmed in a letter it would not withdraw its promise, according to CIWF Director Debbie Tripley.

The court declined another request from the NGOs for access to internal Commission documents. Still, CIWF said the coalition of animal welfare groups would not appeal the case to the Court of Justice of the EU.

Animal Welfare Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi told a group of EU lawmakers Tuesday that “the Commission will study the judgment and we will comply with it in the best possible way.”

The current assembly of commissioners set out plans this year to phase out cages for chickens and pigs, but there are not clear timelines for other animal groups included in Wednesday’s ruling.

The Commission did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

articles.title: French justice minister opens probe into prosecutor seen at far-right HQ
articles.summary:
PARIS — French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin has ordered an internal investigation to determine why a prosecutor was at Marine Le Pen’s National Rally headquarters when police raided the offices earlier this month.

“We need to clear up a point of ambiguity: Did senior officials provide information to the National Rally, which would obviously be a crime against their office and the high regard they hold for their independence?” Darmanin told France Inter radio on Wednesday.

Christian de Rocquigny, a Paris-based prosecutor, was at the far-right party’s headquarters when police arrived as part of an investigation into allegations that an interior ministry official had leaked confidential judicial information to the National Rally. The official, Hugues Moutouh, has resigned as the senior state representative in the Centre-Val de Loire region and is officially leaving office Wednesday.

De Rocquigny was meeting with Jean-Paul Garraud, a former magistrate who serves as an MEP for the National Rally. Garraud told Franceinfo they had “a conversation between two professionals,” during which they discussed the fight against drug trafficking and did not talk about investigations into the party.

De Rocquigny told the French news agency AFP last week that his presence was unrelated to the case and that he was there to have coffee with an acquaintance who is a party official. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the investigation being announced.

Darmanin said the prosecutor under investigation had mishandled the situation by not informing his superiors that he had been present during the police raid and by going to meet his acquaintance for coffee during work hours without taking leave.

The justice minister stressed that judicial officials must tread carefully around political engagements ahead of a crucial election year. The investigation will need to determine whether any sensitive information was discussed, he added.

articles.title: EU Commission warns budget cuts will leave governments worse off
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin criticized cuts to the EU’s next seven-year budget ahead of a leaders’ summit in Brussels.

During a speech at the European Parliament on Wednesday morning, Serafin warned that the €44 billion of cuts European Council President António Costa presented last Saturday will leave EU governments worse off.

“Cutting the Union budget will not necessarily bring savings for our member states,” Serafin said. “They will have to bear the costs of investments in competition and security anyway through national budgets.”

His remarks set the scene for tough discussions among leaders on Thursday and Friday. One EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak freely, said this was likely to be a “bloody” European Council as governments are not ready to compromise on their red lines.

Costa is keen to make progress in negotiations ahead of another summit on the Multiannual Financial Framework starting on Dec. 17. But EU governments are divided over the total size of the budget, with Germany leading a push to shave off further tens of billions from the Commission’s proposal.  

“Further substantial cuts are needed to reduce the massive increases compared with the current MFF to a reasonably affordable level,” the German government wrote in an internal note seen by POLITICO.

Berlin also renewed calls to reintroduce discounts on the budget contributions from wealthier countries, known as rebates. “It is a basic prerequisite for any agreement,” it wrote.

But in a more conciliatory move, Germany said it will examine a proposed EU-wide tax on digital giants “with an open mind.”

Serafin dismissed claims that the size of the EU budget is increasing. He argued instead that the proposal on the table is lower than the current seven-year budget that entered into force in 2021 as a share of gross national income.

“Some keep pretending that the budget still increases as compared to the current MFF,” he said. “But that is only because they do not factor in inflation — and that is simply not convincing.”

The Commission wrote in a note Tuesday that, based on the latest inflation estimates, the proposal amounts to 1.06% of the EU’s GNI. The figure shrinks to 0.97% excluding the repayments of the bloc’s post-Covid debt.

Sebastian Starcevic contributed to this report.

articles.title: Kommission will 50-Milliarden-Euro-Fonds zur Förderung europäischer Schlüsseltechnologie aufsetzen
articles.summary:
BRÜSSEL – Die Europäische Kommission plant, direkte Beteiligungen in Höhe von mehreren hundert Millionen Euro an einheimischen Technologieunternehmen zu erwerben, um sie in europäischer Hand zu halten. Den Plan für den Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF) stellte die EU-Kommission am Mittwoch vor.

Der Fonds soll ein Volumen von insgesamt 50 Milliarden Euro erreichen. Mit öffentlichen Mitteln der EU, der Mitgliedstaaten und von Partnern wie der Europäischen Investitionsbank (EIB) soll privates Kapital für Investitionen in Schlüsseltechnologien mobilisiert werden.

Das Ziel sei es, Technologien zu fördern, die für die „technologische Souveränität und wirtschaftliche Sicherheit“ der Union von entscheidender Bedeutung sind, erklärte ein Vertreter der Kommission gegenüber Reportern.

„Wir müssen öffentliche Mittel effizienter als Katalysator einsetzen, um privates Kapital anzuziehen“, fügte der Beamte hinzu.

Die EU-Beauftragte für technologische Souveränität, Henna Virkkunen, hatte letzte Woche erklärt, sie wolle 50 Milliarden Euro als „Ausgangspunkt“ für den Fonds, ein Ziel, das zum Beispiel der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron unterstützt hat.

Der Vorschlag für den Fonds ist jedoch noch nicht vollständig ausgearbeitet. Er hängt vom nächsten siebenjährigen Haushalt der EU ab, über den die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU derzeit verhandeln, unter anderem auf einer Sitzung des Europäischen Rates am Donnerstag und Freitag.

Im neuen „Quantum Act“ der EU, der ebenfalls am Mittwoch vorgestellt wurde, findet sich bereits ein Verweis auf den Fonds: Darin wird „Eigenkapitalfinanzierung für strategische Quantenunternehmen und -projekte im Rahmen von STEF“ zugesagt.

Quantum-Unternehmen „finden oft das Kapital zum Wachsen und Expandieren außerhalb von Europa“, warnte der Vertreter.

Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass die Europäische Kommission als Anteilseigner an Technologieunternehmen auftritt. EU-Mittel werden bereits im Europäischen Innovationsrat (EIC) und im Scaleup Europe Fund (SEF) eingesetzt, doch diese sind für kleinere Investitionen vorgesehen (bis zu 30 Millionen Euro für den EIC; bis zu 300 Millionen Euro für den SEF).

„Was in diesem Umfeld fehlt, sind daher größere Finanzierungen unserer strategischen Unternehmen“, sagte der Vertreter.

articles.title: 18 brilliant and surprising gifts for science lovers this Christmas
articles.summary:
This moon lamp is a hot Christmas tip from designer Phoebe Watts (see below)

Gingko Design

The New Scientist Christmas gift guide is assembled by our crack team of science editors and experts. If you’re struggling for gift ideas, you will find unexpected and ingenious suggestions for amateur astronomers and animal and nature lovers, as well as those fond of food, beauty and puzzles. And surely that covers all of us?

Space reporter Leah Crane recommends the science-themed jigsaws from Nervous System

Nervous System

Puzzlingly beautiful: a science jigsaw

If you’re looking for a quick and easy jigsaw to breeze through while watching holiday movies, Nervous System puzzles probably aren’t for you. But if you want something that’s part puzzle, part work of art, and that will keep you transfixed for hours, they’ll definitely do the trick. Nervous System makes laser-cut wooden puzzles with uniquely shaped pieces and science themes, and they are absolutely beautiful. I’m particularly a fan of their geode puzzles, featuring concentric wiggles of bright colour, including wiggly sides that defy every puzzler’s instinct to start with the edge pieces. For even more of a challenge, they make infinity puzzles that can be assembled and reassembled many different ways – those have no edge pieces at all, and some don’t even have a picture on them! Nervous System also sells absolutely stunning jewellery, lamps and sculptures, but to me the puzzles are the real show-stoppers.

Nervous System puzzles, from $45 (£32)

Advertisement

Leah Crane

The CL Companion 8×30 binoculars, as recommended by senior editor Chelsea Whyte

Swarovski Optik

Zoom in: splashing out on binoculars

The eccentric filmmaker Werner Herzog famously declared that he travels with only a second set of underwear, a map, a toothbrush and a set of binoculars. I don’t travel quite so lightly, but on my next trip, I definitely want to add a pair of nice binos to my baggage. I tested out three sets at varying price levels, taking them down to my favourite spot on my local river and out to my backyard during a clear night with a half-moon overhead. The Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 binoculars are extremely well balanced and were the most comfortable in my hands. They were particularly well-suited for twilight and brighter. The other Nikon set I tried was the Stabilised 12×25 S, which is much more compact. For my small hands that was fine, and the stabilisation was marvellous at reducing any shaking, both while looking at something fixed like the moon or moving quickly to track an eagle fishing for dinner. The stabilisation requires batteries, so these are probably best –suited to the more prepared adventurer. The stand–out pair was the CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik. I’ve never seen anything look better than they did through these lenses. They let in an enormous amount of light, making the world look like the brightness has been turned up. And the moon’s craters looked stunningly crisp. For the birdwatcher, wildlife lover or stargazer in your life, these would be a worthwhile, although pretty major, splurge.

Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42, £159

Nikon Stabilised 12×25 S, £729

CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik, from £1070

Chelsea Whyte

Podcast editor Rowan Hooper’s tip this Christmas: the Magenta 5 bat detector

Widcare

Sounds good: a bat detector

Thomas Nagel’s famous 1974 essay, “What is it like to be a bat?”, argued that we can never fully know the experience of being a bat (or any other animal). I have been testing that argument with my fantastic bat detector. The device picks up on the ultrasound frequencies emitted by bats as they fly overhead and converts them into clicks that we can hear. It also displays the frequency of the squeak, and that allows us to identify the species. In my London back garden I get mostly pipistrelles, our smallest bat at just 4 grams. Nagel is right – I don’t know what it is like to fly and catch moths by echolocation. But it is quite thrilling to hear the clicks as a bat swoops past in the dark, and that experience has got me a little closer to appreciating what it is like to be a bat. There are several options available, but I used the Magenta 5 bat detector from Wildcare.

Magenta 5 bat detector, £105

Rowan Hooper

Editor Catherine de Lange recommends the Timeshifter app

Natee Meepian/Timeshifter

Time for bed: a jet lag app

If you have a jetsetter in your life, they are probably by definition the kind of person who is tricky to find a gift for. So why not gift them something money can’t buy (well, almost): an end to jet lag? Many moons ago, I was on a journalism fellowship about sleep at Harvard Medical School, when I visited the lab of sleep scientist Steven Lockley. I was fascinated by his experiments, including work he was doing with NASA astronauts, which looked at circadian rhythms, sleep and what happens when our bodies are out of sync with the natural rhythms of the day. Aside from astronauts, many of us who remain earthbound can still feel these effects – especially those who do regular shift work or long-distance travel. What’s more, a body clock that’s out of whack can have serious health consequences.

I followed Lockley’s research closely over the years, and he was generous enough, whenever I travelled back to Boston, to make me a tailored jet-lag plan – when to sleep or nap in the days before and during my flight, as well as when to wear sunglasses and drink caffeine, all based on what time my flight was and the time difference. Fast forward about a decade, and this service is no longer a personal one – Lockley has created an app called Timeshifter, which allows users to plug in their flight details and instantly receive a step-by-step plan to minimise jet lag. There’s a version of the app for shift workers, too.

I recently tried it on a trip to New York, purchasing a one-off plan rather than the subscription, and I can honestly say that I barely felt any jet lag at all – while my husband was falling asleep in his sushi at dinner.

Timeshifter app, $6.99/month or $69.99/year (£5.30/month or £53/year)

Catherine de Lange

Environment reporter Madeleine Cuff recommends the Motus Strength II trainers

Vivobarefoot

Strong feet: barefoot trainers

Forget spin classes and aerobics – fitness these days is all about strength over heart rate. If a loved one has started talking about “Lifting PBs” and “protein-maxxing”, you could do much worse than getting them some proper footwear for their gym trips. There’s emerging evidence to suggest barefoot trainers strengthen foot muscles compared with regular trainers, including the small, stabilising muscles that improve balance. Vivobarefoot’s Motus Strength are specifically designed for weightlifting sessions – I’ve been wearing them to the gym for the last few weeks and am a total convert. You can also get barefoot shoes for hiking and trail running, for those who prefer the great outdoors to the weights floor.

Vivobarefoot Motus Strength, £150

Madeleine Cuff

Video editor Emily Bates is enjoying these animal trading cards

Life TGC

Collect them all: animal trading cards

If, like me, you grew up collecting Pokémon cards but now shudder at the prices and scalpers, there’s a brilliant alternative, and it’s science-themed. Life TCG lets players collect, trade and play using cards based on real-world creatures, with gameplay reminiscent of Top Trumps. But the artwork is the real highlight, a charming mix of realistic paintings, quirky cartoons and special-edition photography. One of my first packs even revealed a stunning South Chinese tiger card (one of my favourite animals). The gameplay itself is fairly simple, but the cards are beautiful enough to work as collectible art pieces in their own right. Better still, first-edition holographic cards are genuinely rare. Each is printed in numbers matching that animal’s estimated population in the wild. Life TCG also donates a portion of its profits to WWF. Collecting cards that look great, teach you something and support wildlife conservation? That’s a rare win.

Life TCG cards, from £15

Emily Bates

Cheers: a guide to the glories of wine

For more than 8000 years (in between struggling to survive), humans have been harvesting and fermenting grapes to make the delicious liquid we call wine. Over that time, we’ve amassed more knowledge about this plant-based product than any other – except the secrets of what gives a wine its distinctive quality. Noble Nine is a state-of-the-art guide to that quest and many other things vinous by researcher Andrew Wood – perhaps the only academic anywhere lucky enough to do a PhD in the biology of wine quality. Our first metaphorical glass comes from the merlot wine grape, and we cheerfully drink our way through the other eight in Wood’s selection, including chenin blanc, pinot noir, shiraz, and ending up with sauvignon blanc. Cheers, everyone!

Noble Nine: The story and science of the world’s favourite wines by Andrew Wood, £20

Liz Else

Fresh herbs will be a regular treat with the AUK Mini 2.0 indoor herb garden, says Madeleine Cuff

AUK

Herbs on tap: an indoor herb garden

I’ve got a little herb garden outside on my patio, and there’s no better feeling during the warmer months than popping out to fetch some fresh coriander or basil midway through dinner prep. But in the winter, I usually rely on plastic packets of supermarket herbs, which inevitably wilt in the fridge before I use them all. The solution? An indoor herb garden that lets you grow fresh herbs all year round. I’ve tested a few models, and the Auk Mini 2 is the winner for easy setup, stylish design and bountiful harvest. It fits on a shelf in my kitchen and costs about 50p per week to run.

Auk Mini 2, £209

Madeleine Cuff

The Bambu Lab A1 mini 3D Printer, as recommended by Catherine de Lange’s ten-year-old son

Bambu Lab

Make your own: a 3D printer

For my son’s 10th birthday, his grandmother wanted to gift him a very extravagant present – a 3D printer. I wasn’t convinced at first, worried it would be too big for the house, too technical, dangerous (who wants to let their kids play with melting plastic?) and generally a bad idea. A few months in, I’m happy to be recommending this as a great present for a very special young person in your life. We went for the Bambu Labs A1 mini, which is small enough to be stored out of sight and brought out for supervised use. So far, it’s been very easy to “plug and play”, and my son has printed a range of plastic tat that nobody needed, and a couple of “gifts” for me, including a stand for my phone while I cook (how thoughtful!). Now that we’ve grasped the basics, the next step is for him to learn to design his own projects, which is where things become more educational. I’m also hoping we can use it to print spare parts when appliances break at home. Unlike toys that get played with a few times and forgotten, a 3D printer is a gift that can evolve with your child’s abilities and get used for years to come.

Bambu Labs A1 mini 3D printer, £139

Catherine de Lange

A voucher for a sound bath like this one is features editor Olivia Goldhill’s top tip for a Christmas gift

Emra Sound Healing

Sound choice: a sound bath voucher

Feeling yourself immersed in the deep vibrations of a singing bowl isn’t just a pleasant acoustic experience. Sound baths – when you listen, usually while lying down, to acoustic instruments –are deeply, deeply relaxing. Studies have found the experience helps reduce feelings of anxiety and tension, and there’s also evidence they can improve both sleep and cognitive function. Sound baths are a meditative practice and that, for me, is where the true benefits lie. Silent meditation is difficult, and it’s hard not to grow frustrated with myself for my wandering thoughts and inability to focus on my breath. The beautiful music of sound baths provides an external, soothing distraction. They provide a space to pause and allow to-do lists to gently fade away. There are both private and group-class sound baths, either of which would make a thoughtful gift as a shared activity or simply a new year’s reset.

Sound bath vouchers, from £25 (A few options in London, Brighton & Manchester)

Olivia Goldhill

Head of books Alison Flood is recommending this guide to surviving the apocalypse

Disaster ready: a guide to rebuilding civilisation

A regular topic of conversation when I get together with my wider family is how we would survive in the event of an apocalypse, and who would contribute what skills. With my husband an engineer, my brother-in-law a doctor and my mum a brilliant gardener, we think we’d do pretty well, but I’ve decided the key thing I’d contribute is my copy of The Book. Subtitled “the ultimate guide to rebuilding civilization”, it covers everything from making fire and beer to leathercraft and traps. Running to 400 pages, it was written with the scientific and technical advice of Lewis Dartnell at the University of Westminster, UK, and would be a fun and practical gift for anyone in your life who is eyeing the future with trepidation.

The Book, £99

Alison Flood

Rowan Hooper also recommends this mushroom growing kit from Merryhill Mushrooms

Merryhill Mushrooms

Grow your own: a mushroom-growing kit

It is widely accepted that growing your own fruit and vegetables is not only mentally rewarding, but that the food tastes especially good when the gap between picking it and eating it is minimised. But, I thought, what about mushrooms? To find out, I grew my own mushrooms with foolproof growing kits from Merryhill Mushrooms. Choose the species of mushroom, and the company delivers the kit to your door. I tried regular chestnut mushrooms and the impressive lion’s mane mushroom. You really don’t have to do much other than keep their box humid; within a couple of weeks, the mushrooms had emerged from the mycelial mass, and I had picked and eaten them. Mushroom steaks and “pulled shroom” curry. Delicious!

Mushroom growing kit from Merryhill Mushrooms, from £18.95

Rowan Hooper

Designer Phoebe Watts loves the moon lamp she splurged on

Gingko Design

Lunar magic: a moon lamp

Last year, I stumbled upon the Space store in the Oxford covered market, drawn in by the floating, spinning globes in the window display. The thing that particularly caught my eye was a true 3D-printed model of the moon, suspended by a magnet – it looked like it defied gravity. I subsequently splashed out and bought it! It’s now a great addition to my desk and has become something I really love. The model is raised so that the surface is textured, and you can interact with it a bit. The globe also has three light tones (warm, cool and neutral), which is great for setting a mood. You can get it slightly cheaper elsewhere but if you can, I would highly suggest supporting the Space store. And if this one can’t be justified, they have many other cool products and globe lights that don’t float.

Smart moon lamp, £159

Phoebe Watts

Madeleine Cuff has another Christmas tip: CleanOil’s green beauty products

Raven Botanicals

Green pampering: innovative body oil

Vegetable oils are in almost everything, from beauty products and sandwiches to even pet food. But producing them requires a huge amount of land, energy and water. Clean Food Group is an exciting British company working to change that, using precision fermentation to produce oils from yeast in vats. It estimates its CleanOil product offers a 90 per cent cut to carbon emissions compared with using palm oil. Scottish beauty company Raven Beauty became the first company to use CleanOil in consumer products this year, releasing a facial cleanser in September, which I road-tested for a New Scientist video. Now Raven has released a range of body oils also featuring CleanOil, which would make a great gift for someone who deserves a bit of pampering. Plus, I think this small company deserves a cheer for being one of the first in line for pioneering green technology.

Body oil, £38

Madeleine Cuff

Catherine de Lange also recommends this book as a personalised Christmas gift

Fact and Story

Pinning you down: Your life in data

We may be used to talking about how many times around the sun we have travelled each birthday. But for the inquisitive-minded, there’s more detail to be had. Have you stopped to consider, for instance, how many volcanoes have erupted since the day you were born, or how many times your heart has beaten? How many dinosaurs were named in that time, or elements discovered?

This is the premise behind Days of You, a beautiful and personalised hardback book, packed full of data specifically tailored to a specific person. All you have to do is provide the name, date of birth and place of birth of your special someone, and the team behind Days of You (which, incidentally, is the brainchild of former New Scientist staffer Matt Walker) pulls together stats and data ranging from the shape of the moon on the birthday in question to what the price of tea and the best-selling album were that year. This is essentially a beautifully visualised piece of data journalism, where the subject is your lucky recipient.

It may sound simple, but much of the data is hard to come by – especially from some of the weather stations – and must be tailored to the birth location in question. For that reason, the book is only available for those born in the US and the UK.

Books usually take 5-6 working days from order to door, the team says, but to be sure, they recommend ordering by 10 December. They also make personalised calendars, mugs, and prints for new babies.

The Days of You, £49

Catherine de Lange

The Brick physical app blocker – as recommended by Madeleine Cuff

Brick

Distraction blocker: a Brick tile

Teenagers usually come in for the most scrutiny over phone use, but the truth is we could all do with cutting back on our screen time, no matter our age. Have a chat with your nearest and dearest about their New Year’s resolutions and see if reducing their phone use comes up. If it does, a Brick might be the perfect gift this Christmas. It’s a small magnetic tile, and when you tap your phone against it, a pre-selected group of apps is blocked from use until you tap again. I use mine to curb scrolling during work hours and reduce my phone use around my children at the weekend. I’ve found the extra effort it takes to go and find the Brick to tap and unlock your apps has been enough to rewire my behaviour pretty significantly. Brick has also just launched Brick Night, which blocks selected apps from being used when you enter your bedroom – perfect for preventing doomscrolling before bed.

Brick, £49, Brick Night,  £119

Madeleine Cuff

articles.title: Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial
articles.summary:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Read more

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

Advertisement

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective, it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Health Check

Sign up to newsletter

In the clinical trial, 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney, the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

Read more

You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a trial of KT-621 in people with asthma, since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

articles.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
articles.summary:
A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November

AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Read more

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

Read more

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

Read more

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.
