articles.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother: the sacred and profane collide in this off-kilter hitman drama
articles.summary:
A grieving widower with three children and a dwindling supply of frozen breast milk is an unlikely premise for a crime thriller. Yet this is where Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother begins, moving between the intimate demands of fatherhood and a criminal underworld populated by characters who might have stepped from the pages of a comic book.

Director Bassam Tariq’s latest film has moments of domestic tenderness sitting alongside brutal violence, with strange flashes of black humour emerging in the most unexpected places.

Mahershala Ali plays Latif, a devout Muslim and hitman struggling to raise his three children following the death of his wife. In their cramped Texas flat, teenage daughter Fatiha (Adia), eight-year-old Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) and baby Aziza are adjusting to life without their mother. Heartbreakingly, the supply of his late wife’s frozen breast milk is running out, and the baby cannot tolerate formula. This affecting detail highlights the mother’s absence in the daily routines of a household still dependent upon her.

Ali brings an effortless gravity to Latif. Physically imposing yet remarkably still, he conveys a man weighed down by guilt and the responsibilities of fatherhood. There is an economy to his movements which lends poignancy to even the smallest domestic encounters. His capacity for violence appears incongruous with this quiet presence, until he is drawn back into the work he knows.

Crime boss Mike (Laith Nakli) orders Latif to kill Pastor Hwan (John Cho), a former Marine leading a heavily armed group of Christian fundamentalists. Hwan has threatened Mike’s nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali), who runs a pornography and sex work operation. These figures are grotesque and absurd, verging on caricature, sometimes provoking uneasy laughter with their excesses.

At the heart of the film is Adia’s compelling performance as Fatiha. On the cusp of adulthood, she is beginning to test the boundaries of her independence, even as her mother’s absence places increasing demands upon her at home. The pull of a life beyond the family competes with the needs of her younger siblings. Adia’s emotional intensity gives these domestic tensions a rawness which feels entirely authentic.

Faith and violence

The film frequently draws the sacred and profane together in provocative imagery. Latif’s Muslim faith is deeply held, shaping his daily rituals and sense of moral responsibility, though his work as a hired killer presents an uncomfortable contradiction.

His choice of a sword over a gun adds an almost surreal quality to the violence, particularly against the film’s contemporary setting. Pastor Hwan offers a more twisted, fanatical expression of religious belief, using his Christian fundamentalism to justify brutality.

Tariq had originally planned to work with Ali on Marvel’s Blade which was cancelled during development. Certainly, Ali’s acrobatic and inventive sword work in the fight scenes wouldn’t have looked out of place in Marvel’s scrapped vampire-slayer movie. These big fight scenes can jar when juxtaposed with tender moments, but Ali has the presence to pull it off with aplomb, creating an oddly unsettling atmosphere.

Tariq’s cinematography and soundtrack add to this disquiet. Inverted views of the city render familiar streets strange, while the soundtrack occasionally evokes religious chanting. These unexpected flourishes add to the film’s peculiar, off-kilter sensibility.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother occasionally feels uneven. The tonal shifts between domestic realism and outlandish violence are not always comfortably resolved. Tariq’s appetite for the grotesque sometimes threatens to overwhelm the more affecting family drama, though there is much to admire in the film’s refusal to shy away from its own peculiarities.

It is in the relationships between Latif and his children, and the bonds that hold them together in their mother’s absence, that the film finds its greatest strength. There is bloodshed and violence aplenty, but who would have thought the hardest thing to watch would be a little spilled breast milk.

Laura O'Flanagan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Why Taiwanese firms are reluctant to leave China, even as tensions rise
articles.summary:
When Stan Shih, the founder of electronics company Acer, arrived in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen to represent Taiwan at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit recently, his company was already in the news.

Acer and fellow Taiwanese computer maker Asus were reportedly moving some production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China. Rising memory-chip costs globally had made computers more expensive to build, and Chinese manufacturers could offer lower prices.

At the same summit, Chinese president Xi Jinping raised Taiwan in talks with his US counterpart, Donald Trump. Xi urged Trump to “do the right thing” on Taiwan, warning that any major disruption over the island could damage relations between Beijing and Washington.

Beijing claims the democratically governed island as its own and, while maintaining it prefers peaceful “reunification”, has not ruled out using military force to bring Taiwan under its control. China regularly conducts military and naval drills around the island.

Yet many Taiwanese entrepreneurs in China, known as Taishang, are reluctant to leave as long as their Chinese operations remain viable. Some are building up operations elsewhere to reduce their exposure to political pressure as tensions rise.

Staying in China is not just about costs or customers. For many of the entrepreneurs I have interviewed, it is also about keeping people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in contact when relations between their governments are strained.

Less investment does not mean leaving

Taiwanese firms helped fuel China’s economic miracle in the 1990s and 2000s by building factories to supply overseas markets. They made everything from footwear in Dongguan to laptops in Kunshan, near Shanghai. Later, as US tariffs made it harder to export from China to the US, some Taiwanese firms turned to Chinese buyers to keep their factories running.

China’s share of Taiwanese outbound investment has gradually fallen. In 2010, mainland China received nearly 84% of Taiwan’s approved outward investment. By 2025, its share had sunk to 3.8%. But that tells us where Taiwanese companies are putting new money, not whether they are closing factories or giving up on Chinese customers.

At the end of March 2026, about two-thirds of Taiwan’s publicly traded companies still had investments in mainland China. Together, these companies earned NT$145 billion (£3.35 billion) from those investments in the first three months of the year.

As part of a so-called “China+1” strategy, some Taiwanese firms are expanding abroad while continuing to invest in China. In October, Taiwanese circuit board materials maker Ventec opened its first factory in Thailand and committed about US$50 million (£38 million) to expand in Kunshan.

The plants serve different needs. Thailand gives Ventec another base to supply industries such as aerospace and medical technology, while the Kunshan expansion lets it add capacity quickly as demand grows for materials used in AI hardware. A second site also gives Ventec options if conditions change in either location. Many Taiwanese companies think that way.

At the same time, Chinese officials are giving Taiwanese firms more reasons to stay. In 2023, Beijing designated the south-eastern province of Fujian a pilot zone for closer economic ties with Taiwan. But the courtship extends well beyond Fujian.

At a business forum held in China’s Anhui province in 2024, participants signed agreements for 47 Taiwanese-funded manufacturing projects, including in electric vehicles. And an AI forum in Kunshan in August 2026 brought together hundreds of entrepreneurs from both sides.

Staying does not mean taking sides

Taiwanese firms can take up these opportunities without sharing Beijing’s goal of unification. In my years of fieldwork with Taiwanese entrepreneurs in China, I’ve often heard the same golden rule: “Never leave the Chinese market.”

Once you’re out, you never get back in. Leaving means more than closing a factory. Customers switch to competitors, and supplier relationships built up over years fall apart. If firms try to return, they have to start from scratch.

Many Taishang I interviewed over the years went back to Taiwan to vote but rarely discussed their political views in public on the mainland. Keeping quiet helps protect their businesses.

It does not mean they back Beijing. Nor are they indifferent to what happens across the Taiwan Strait. Many firmly believe that doing business together can ease tensions by building amicable relationships between people on both sides. They see value in keeping those ties alive even when their governments are at odds.

As one experienced Taishang recently told me, echoing a view I’ve heard from many others: “Chinese and Taiwanese people have no problems with one another. It’s politics that drives us apart. As long as people meet, speak and work together, they can deepen their mutual understanding, and this helps maintain peace across the Taiwan Strait.”

Taiwanese electronics firm Foxconn’s factory in Shenzhen.
Tada Images / Shutterstock

But keeping politics out of the conversation does not keep it out of the factory. In 2021, after Chinese authorities penalised Taiwan’s Far Eastern Group conglomerate over alleged regulatory violations, Beijing warned Taiwanese firms to distance themselves from supporters of formal independence.

Washington can narrow their options, too. As the Shenzhen summit unfolded, Reuters reported that Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC had paused some orders for advanced chips from Chinese customers after the US tightened its export rules. Yet turning down some orders is not the same as giving up the market. TSMC still runs factories in China.

The Taishang remain both a risk and an opportunity for Taiwan, as they have always been. They do not readily comply with repeated demands from their own government and US authorities to move their operations out of China. This contributes to Taiwan’s economic and political exposure to China.

But the Taishang keep people on both sides working together and, arguably, understanding each other. This cannot guarantee peace between China and Taiwan, but helps to maintain channels of contact that no summit can create on its own.

Gunter Schubert receives funding from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG).

articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.

Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.

At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 lets players respawn – a new prison art exhibition shows what happens when you can’t
articles.summary:
When Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA), the latest entry in the best-selling video game franchise, was announced, UK workers reportedly booked off 83,000 days of annual leave just to be among the first to step into its criminal underworld.

Players hijack cars, orchestrate heists and outrun the law – knowing that if things go wrong, they simply respawn. Yet in the real world, many of the offences that drive GTA’s missions account for over 80,000 immediate custodial sentences a year across England and Wales, where there is no reset button.

This widening gap between the thrill of fictional crime and the grim reality of confinement sits at the heart of our latest collaboration between the University of Hull and HMP Hull. As researchers and prison educators working together on the project, we wanted to explore how creative arts can challenge media stereotypes of crime while supporting prisoner wellbeing – work we have also captured in a short documentary about the collaboration.

The free ACCT Exhibition, which is displayed in the university’s art gallery, challenges media representations of crime, justice and injustice. Using artwork and poetry, prisoners have creatively responded to University of Hull research on confinement, control and surveillance.

The exhibition’s full title, Artistic Comments on Carceral Thematics, is a play on the use of the acronym ACCT (Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork). This is a vital process in prisons in England and Wales that monitors and supports the mental wellbeing of prisoners – specifically those at serious risk of self-harm and suicide.

The artists serving at HMP Hull named the exhibition in this way to demonstrate how the creative arts can help people serving sentences to cope with life inside.

From controller to canvas

In 2026, in the art classroom at HMP Hull, a young man on remand awaiting sentencing worked on his first ever piece of artwork. His paintings were representations of his experience, from crime to prison in the style of GTA’s graphics.

He created these paintings having spoken with one of our team, James McLean, who was interested in the glamorisation of crime through video games. This young artist felt comfortable painting these images because for him, GTA’s world was his world.

Four large-scale paintings based around the game HMP Hull feature in the wider exhibition. Working in collaboration with his teacher, the artist was interested in shifting the accepted narrative of receiving rewards for completing crime-related missions. The paintings in this part of the exhibition show the realities and consequences of such a lifestyle. Accompanying the paintings on the gallery wall is a written explanation of the work:

Even though we have captured the vibrancy and the energy of the game and the “glamourous” life of crime in our work, we have also inserted the moral implications into the story. We have endeavoured to show the reality and the grim conclusion to such a life.

While research shows that playing violent video games is not associated with aggressive behaviour, GTA, like other representations of crime, can potentially glamourise wealth, power and apparent invincibility. This mirrors some real-world drivers of criminal behaviour, particularly motivations rooted in consumer culture and a desire for status and belonging.

True crime, meanwhile, frequently glamourises the way people come to find themselves serving a prison sentence. Researchers have noted that audiences often side with the offender – so long as they are charismatic. Indeed, numerous TV and film hits have centred on offenders, such as Tommy Shelby of Peaky Blinders, Tony Soprano of The Sopranos or Vito Corleone of The Godfather.

But many prisoners have themselves been victims of emotional, physical and sexual abuse during childhood among other adverse childhood experiences. And a high proportion of the prison population have mental health illnesses in comparison to the general population. Because so many people enter prison carrying trauma and poor mental health, finding ways to support their wellbeing inside is critical.

The ACCT Exhibition has created an opportunity to open up conversations about systems of control and coercion that remain unfamiliar to many people. It also highlights the potential of creative practice to support the wellbeing of people serving prison sentences through meaningful activity.

By replacing the fantasy of a quick respawn with the reality of confinement, these artists are proving that while there is no reset button in the criminal justice system, there is still room to rewrite the ending.

The ACCT Exhibition is on display at the University of Hull Art Gallery until December 31 2026

The authors would like to acknowledge the vital roles of the HMP Hull project leads, Jamie Smith and Kristian Wealsby. The authors and the HMP Hull project leads form the leadership team of the ACCT Exhibition project.

James McLean and Josephine Metcalf do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: The rotters of Rutshire, the Bloomsbury set and loving Lorca: what to watch, see and read this week
articles.summary:
I’m really enjoying the fact that most people I know who watch Rivals have dropped the “just my guilty pleasure” shtick and now simply confess to full-on loving it.

My own residual guilt stems from the fact that when I was a teenager, my mother, who grew up reading Austen, Dickens and the Brontës, was profoundly disappointed and filled with sorrow to catch me with well-thumbed copies of Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire nonsense. But they were so funny and rude, and also I was horse-mad and a member of the local pony club, so it all just seemed such a good fit. I even went to a fancy ball once in a glittery sequinned boob-tube and thought I was the height of sophistication. Well, it was the 1980s.

Part two of season two picks up after a particularly dramatic part one cliffhanger. Spoiler alert! After discovering the latest affair of her husband Tony (a gloriously nasty David Tennant), long-suffering wife and all-round good egg Monica (Claire Rushbrook) sweeps out of the house in a storm, buckled with grief and humiliation. She somehow finds her windblown way to the house of Lizzie (Katherine Parkinson), also wife to a faithless husband, James (the marvellous Oliver Chris giving hilarious half-Partridge-half-Madeley vibes). The two sit down for a comforting cup of tea, and quickly graduate to the brandy bottle.

But then something extraordinary happens. After her King Lear moment in the storm, Monica is spent and becalmed, and the two women begin to examine the symmetry of their lives with ghastly men who take them for granted. In this scene, says our reviewer Claudine van Hensbergen, the “two frumpiest and most downtrodden women in Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire become the beating heart of the episode – perhaps the whole series”.

It’s Rivals as domestic tragedy, a moment of liberation for two women who realise they would not wish their lives for their own daughters. This poignant scene is the catalyst for change as two worn-down housewives become heroines.

Read more:
Rivals season two: why a shocking death in episode six changes everything for the women of Rutshire

From Moomins to Bloomsbury

The recent release of The Hobbit illustrated by Tove Jansson marks the first time a full edition of the Finn’s Tolkien illustrations has appeared in English. Of course Jansson is best known for the Moomin tales which she both wrote and illustrated.

But anyone familiar with her early illustrations will understand how perfectly her style lent itself to Tolkien’s elvish epic. The imaginations of both Tolkien and Jansson were fundamentally shaped by Finnish myth and folklore, and there are many similarities between the rendering of her own Moomins and Tolkien’s Hobbit characters.

Read more:
Tove Jansson’s illustrations for The Hobbit capture the ‘ecstatic truth’ of childhood

The originality of painters Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – central figures of the Bloomsbury set – is often sensationalised, with most focus directed on their unconventional sex lives as much as their modernist art. Now a new show at London’s Tate, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury attempts to redress the balance and turn that focus back on the art of this fascinating couple.

On show are more than 300 works that trace the couple’s 50-year creative partnership and visitors can enjoy a full restaging of their studio from Charleston, their exquisite house in Sussex.

Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Inside Bloomsbury is on at Tate Britain, London till 11 April 2027.

Read more:
Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury looks beyond the sex to the art – with mixed results

For the love of Lorca

I am so looking forward to watching Spanish film La Bola Negra (The Black Ball). The title comes from the last unfinished play of Federico García Lorca, considered Spain’s most influential 20th-century poet and playwright. This luminous talent was snuffed out when Lorca was executed by firing squad in 1936 at the start of the Spanish civil war, after being imprisoned for his politics and his homosexuality.

Lorca’s unfinished text is a seed that grows and expands into the 21st century, marking three moments in Spain’s history: the second republic in 1932, the civil war in 1937, and contemporary Spain in 2017, taking in three gay stories along the way.

La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

Read more:
La Bola Negra: this deeply moving cinematic homage to Lorca is part of his queer legacy

You Can See Everything is another film I can’t wait to see, which says quite a lot for a three-hour documentary about someone I know very little of. The film has had critics raving as Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder decamps to the house of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of medical company Theranos, in her last days of freedom before she is sent to prison.

Holmes was convicted of fraud after it was discovered that the claims of her blood-testing technology were bogus. Fielder gets literally right in the face of the strange, inscrutable Holmes, who claims she can’t really understand where things went wrong.

In this piece, business academics Kate Kenny and Susi Geiger draw our attention to how gendered stereotypes have shaped Holmes’s story and urge us to interrogate the biases we hold about women like her as we watch the documentary.

You Can See Everything is in cinemas now.

Read more:
Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything

articles.title: People wade through floodwater because they underestimate danger – how to avoid risk
articles.summary:
A firefighter dealing with an emergency situation in Oxford after significant flooding. Alessia Pierdomenico/Shutterstock

A footpath home disappears beneath brown water. The other side is only a few metres away and someone has already crossed. Turning back means a long detour and you will be late. Would you wade through? This is the kind of everyday decision that flood safety advice must address.

People do not need to be thrill-seekers to enter dangerous water. They may just be trying to get home. But a familiar route can become an unfamiliar hazard within minutes.

Flooding is one of the leading causes of death during climate disasters worldwide. People can underestimate the speed or power of the water, or they might not spot underwater hazards that could mean they trip and fall.

A significant number of deaths are due to avoidable behaviour. There have been some recent UK fatalities during floods, including in 2023, when storm water rose suddenly.

In the US, the second highest cause of deaths during floods is people walking into or near water. The US National Weather Service warns just six inches (15cm) of fast-moving water can knock over an adult.

With the UK likely to see high levels of rainfall this winter, and flood risk increasing, it’s worth asking why people decide to wade through floodwater.

A review of research on behaviour around floodwater identified several reasons. One is just wanting to get to a destination, such as going to work or school. Other factors include people travelling to flooded areas to taking photos of the extremely high water levels. Protecting property or pets and helping others who are in trouble are other reasons. Underestimating danger and being influenced by other people were major themes.

Watching someone wade through flooded water could make you feel reassured, even though their height, strength and route may differ from yours. Previous success at walking through a flooded road can also encourage someone to have another attempt. Yet getting through safely last time tells you little about the current conditions.

Media images of floods sometimes depict people paddling through flooded streets. This can make the scene look recreational. This does not, of course, prove that such pictures cause risky behaviour. But it is a reason for news organisations to explain the hazards of entering flood water alongside them. What looks like harmless fun, of people getting on with life – being resilient despite the flood – in a photograph or clip may conceal a strong current or a missing drain cover. Government advice is not to walk through floodwater and also warns that floodwater could be contaminated.

Read more:
Floods and droughts are both signs of water insecurity – they show up in these four places

Why appearances can be deceptive

Even clear water can deceive us. Refraction, the bending of light as it passes from water into air, makes the bottom of a flood appear closer to the surface. This is why a swimming pool can look shallower than it really is.

In muddy floodwater, the more immediate problem is often that you cannot see the bottom at all. A submerged pavement may end at a kerb, ditch or uncovered drain. Knowing where the path normally goes does not establish that the ground beneath it remains intact. In a recent study of 185 drivers, participants often focused on depth even when asked how they would judge water speed. That study concerned driving, not walking, but it highlights why advice needs to explain both the depth and the flow conditions.

Depth is only part of the danger. Research shows how both water depth and speed of the water flow combine with body size to affect balance. Moving water pushes against the legs and body; as more of it is submerged, buoyancy also reduces our weight pressing feet against the ground, making it easier to slip and fall. For otherwise similar conditions, drag increases roughly with the square of water speed: doubling the speed can mean around four times the pushing force.

You can lose your footing well before the water reaches your thighs. The Environment Agency guidance warns that water around 15cm deep can knock someone over or conceal hazards. This is not a safe wading limit. Even shallower water is not automatically safe, and children or people with limited mobility will face different risks.

Heavy storms hit Monmouth in 2025.

What should make you turn back

Floodwater across your route is itself a reason to stop and find an alternative. You do not need to establish its depth or test its strength with your feet. The government advice is to avoid walking through floodwater altogether.

Rising levels, debris being carried along and water flowing forcefully across a path are additional warning signs. So are heavy rain and flood warnings. These signs call for moving away from danger, not getting closer to investigate. Flash flooding can develop before an official warning arrives.

Still water can also be dangerous. It can hide sharp objects, damaged surfaces and sewage. The advice is to stay away from flooded riverbanks as the ground can become unstable or may have already been eroded away below the water. Keep children away and dogs on leads, and never bypass a closure because another person has done so.

Read more:
A record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK

How a game can help

People can explore what to do in an emergency through a game, the Flooding Mucky Dip, that I developed with Girlguiding, Global Link Education and the Environment Agency. At the moment, we are trialling it with schoolchildren in Leicestershire and Rutland, but it can be used by people of any age. It uses tubs of deliberately clouded water (with tea and coffee dissolved in it) containing cards representing flood risks. Participants retrieve cards from the “muddy water” and discuss actions.

Read more:
Did the hot summer make more people worry about climate change? Here’s what the latest indications show

Players can pause a story about a flooded school route and consider what a character should choose next and what to do. Children playing the game can then discuss why following a friend might feel reasonable, then identify another, safer, option. If floodwater blocks the way, choosing another route avoids having to discover what lies beneath it. Playing the game can help children, or adults, understand flooding dangers. Adults could use it to check whether their household plan works. It’s useful to help identify the dangers floodwater can bring.

Other work I am doing with colleagues also explores how stories and practical activities can help families discuss disrupted journeys, safer alternatives and who might need assistance.

With more heavy rains expected this winter, learning how best to respond to a flood could help people understand more clearly what dangers could lie ahead, and how to avoid them.

Katie Parsons receives funding from the Environment Agency and the UK Research and Innovation.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto represented a satirical vision of America – the absurdity of reality has tipped the game into empathy
articles.summary:
Jason and Lucia are in a fight to survive. Rockstar Games

When gaming studio Rockstar announced that its much-delayed new Grand Theft Auto game (GTA VI) would come out in mid-November, most other large scale studios decided to either hold off or push for an earlier release for their titles to avoid being eclipsed.

Growing up, my experience of the universe started with GTA II (1999), its impressive leap to 3D with GTA III (2001), and then Vice City (2002) and San Andreas (2004), which my friends would play during sleepovers. For many players, GTA simply meant sandbox chaos: stealing cars and indulging in gratuitous mayhem.

As I became an adult gamer, I delved lightly into GTA IV (2008) and V (2013), only to realise that the franchise was technically not an American game. Created in Scotland and developed largely by British studios (though today’s massive global teams make it a truly international production), the franchise built its reputation on a distinctly European caricature of the United States: louder, more violent, hyper-capitalist and absurdly unhinged.

Indeed, beneath the violence lay a sharp, progressive satire that the younger audience sometimes missed.

A reality where an alligator is a weapon

Replaying bits of GTA V made this irony impossible to ignore. There are in-game radio ads promoting cigarettes for children, fossil-fuel monopolies funding anti-green energy campaigns and toxic wellness brands peddling self-loathing. It was an exaggerated fun-house mirror held up to American culture; a culture that has since seemed to step through the looking glass.

Over the past decade, following two terms of Donald Trump’s presidency and a steady escalation of political spectacle, the gap between American reality and Rockstar’s satire has shrunk. We exist in a world where a US president openly muses at a press briefing about injecting disinfectant to counter a deadly virus. Then there was the entirely serious state department run by a tech mogul (Elon Musk) named Doge (The US Department of Government Efficiency) – a nod to the his cryptocurrency, dogecoin, which is named after a viral 2013 dog-themed meme.

You have to ask whether the parody has become reality, or whether reality has simply become a parody of itself.

In media theory, the French philosopher Jean Baudrillard coined the term “hyperreal”: a state in which simulations and exaggerated representations become so pervasive that we can no longer distinguish the copy from the original.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the viral side-by-side images comparing GTA VI’s fictional state of Leonida with real-life news footage from Florida. For years, “Florida man” headlines (an internet trope cataloguing the state’s notoriously bizarre, surreal crime blotters, fuelled largely by Florida’s unusually broad public-records laws) have read like rejected GTA mission briefs. For instance, the story of a Florida man who was charged with assault with a deadly weapon in 2016 after tossing a three-and-a-half-foot alligator through a fast-food drive-thru window. That was real life, not a game.

When the real world already operates at maximum absurdity, how do you satirise it?

Read more:
Grand Theft Auto 6 lets players respawn – a new prison art exhibition shows what happens when you can’t

Early critical consensus around GTA VI points to a striking tonal shift. While players can still cause chaos, if they choose, the game’s narrative pulls in the opposite direction. They are no longer casting players as unhinged sociopaths like GTA V’s Trevor, a volatile, meth-dealing career criminal whose playable storylines leaned into torture, mass rampages and grotesque shock value. Instead, protagonists Jason and Lucia are grounded characters whose ambitions are remarkably modest: surviving, protecting each other and scraping together a decent life.

Critics have even noted how the game subtly nudges players toward empathy, rewarding small, mundane acts of care, like texting a partner, doing a food shop or throwing rubbish in a bin. In this GTA, unprovoked street massacres feel weirdly out of step with the story.

As Rockstar co-studio head Rob Nelson observed in interviews around the release, earlier GTA titles were about the illusion of the American Dream. Today, that dream has shrunk to simply affording a home and looking after your family. In a culture saturated with cynicism, sincerity itself has become the unexpected, almost punk rebellion. It is a bleak take, perhaps, yet also a sign of growth.

This evolution matters far beyond gaming circles. Video games have matured into one of our most revealing cultural barometers. When a blockbuster franchise famous for shock value pivots away from scorched-earth parody toward bittersweet intimacy, it tells us something profound about our current political moment. When reality grows dark and surreal enough on its own, satire no longer needs to be as outrageous.

Gaspard Pelurson does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
